articles.title: Classified material missing from Epstein files, documents suggest
articles.summary: Missing pages and a reference to classified documents contradict the Justice Department's claims about the Epstein files.
articles.body:
Attorney General Todd Blanche has long maintained that the so-called Epstein files, even those kept from the public, contain no secret information related to national security.

When the document releases began last winter, Blanche noted that the Epstein Files Transparency Act authorized withholding information in the interest of national security or foreign policy, but said, "no files are being withheld or redacted on that basis."

"There's not some tranche of super-secret documents about Jeffrey Epstein that we're withholding, we're actually not withholding anything based upon [national defense information]," said Blanche, who was deputy attorney general at the time.

But the contents of at least three documents in the massive tranche of files indicate classified information was included in files collected by the DOJ.

One of the documents shows Blanche's Office of the Deputy Attorney General itself received classified material related to Epstein in March 2025. By law, material can only be classified for national security purposes.

What exactly was classified and why remains a mystery.

The Department of Justice says it collected 6 million pages of material and ultimately released over 3 million of those pages after reviewing for duplication, attorney-client privilege and relevance to Jeffrey Epstein.

Congressional challenges and a lawsuit are casting doubts on the DOJ's claims and demanding the release of more documents that were held back.

Included among the Epstein files is an eight-page timeline of the FBI's New York office's initial efforts last year to track down and deliver its voluminous files to the Justice Department's Washington headquarters.

On March 25, 2025, one document shows delivery of "16 Epstein items to ODAG," referring to the Office of the Deputy Attorney General. Among them, items No. 2 and No. 6 are described as "Epstein Transparency Project - Classified Material" and "CDs with classified materials (x2)."

The Epstein Transparency Project refers to the Justice Department's effort to review the files and redact , withhold or clear them for release. It is not clear what exactly was identified as classified. Each CD was likely capable of holding hundreds of megabytes of material.

Also in the files is an email sent that same day from the unit chief of the National Security Classification Operations Unit — an office whose role is to review FBI documents for classification or declassification. The email includes an attachment labeled "Epstein - Classified Document Memo.docx."

The body of the email says there were three documents "identified that remain classified." One was described as an "FBI document which is classified when see-through." A redaction obscures the unit chief's description of the other two documents.

The identity of the email's recipient is also redacted.

It's also not clear whether the two documents — the email and the list — are referring to the same classified material.

A CBS News analysis of a numerical coding system used by the DOJ to organize the Epstein files offers clues about some of the documents the department has withheld.

The codes don't reveal what's missing, but they do show where gaps exist, raising questions about the DOJ's explanation for why documents were withheld.

Among the missing documents are pages from Epstein's own financial records collected as evidence in a federal prosecution.

Here's how it works: Documents from the Epstein files are labeled with a string of numbers beginning with the letters EFTA stamped on the bottom right-hand corner; EFTA stands for Epstein Files Transparency Act.

Those are called Bates numbers — a common way of organizing massive document batches in legal cases. Every page receives its own number. In the Epstein files, the sequence goes from 1 to 2,858,498, which is the tally of approximately how many pages of documents were released.

According to the DOJ, other documents — including court records and investigative files they've previously released — bring the total to over 3 million.

Alongside the Epstein files' Bates numbers are other, older coding numbers that appear on many documents. This indicates that those documents had previously been used in federal legal cases, potentially collected as part of an earlier subpoena.

For instance, Bates coding on some of the documents is from the Ghislaine Maxwell criminal case and was used to organize files given to Maxwell's legal team ahead of her 2021 trial as part of the discovery process.

Other Bates numbers indicate documents were collected from Epstein's banks, including JPMorgan and Deutsche Bank, during the FBI's investigation into his trafficking activities.

Similar gap analyses have been done in the past by independent researchers.

Finding gaps in these documents is a simple process of counting.

In tens of thousands of instances, the main EFTA number will advance by one but the other Bates numbers advance by two or more. Those gaps indicate pages that had been there before were likely removed at some point after the DOJ obtained them.

Take the images below: The EFTA number advances by one but the JPM-SDNY and SDNY_GM numbers advance by 2, as do the page numbers from the original document.

In another example, a series of around 4,500 images of checks from Epstein's accounts has gaps where 66 of those check images should be. Oftentimes the missing image is only the front or the back of the check, although in several cases both are missing.

Comparing all of these numbers against the final EFTA page numbers, it is possible to calculate that there are tens of thousands of pages of documents that are missing from these sections, with no clear reason why.

"Financial records were not a permissible category for removal," Barbara McQuade, the former U.S. Attorney for the Eastern District of Michigan, told CBS News.

Like every federal prosecutor, she says she is very familiar with Bates numbers. "It's the reason you have Bates numbers, so you notice something like that," she said.

The DOJ hasn't responded to CBS News' recent inquiries about the Epstein files, but it has previously said that every document required to be released by the Epstein Files Transparency Act has been released, and the remaining files were unrelated, privileged, or were duplicative.

Another sequence of Bates numbers that provide a map to where documents were removed appears to be from a preliminary processing of the files.

One large sequence of those have "R1" in between EFTA and the page number.

This R1 numbering is found across approximately 995,000 released pages, between p. 61 and p. 2,214,171 in the files. Each page is also labeled with an EFTA page number.

While the EFTAs are sequential, the R1s have gaps which range from 1 page to hundreds of pages. Each time a gap appears — for example, if the EFTA advances by 1 but the R1 advances by 2 — it's evidence that pages were removed.

By comparing these sequences it's possible to identify gaps where documents, mostly emails, were removed between that earlier review and the final release. No partial emails turned up in the thousands of documents we examined, so the removals appear to be entire email exchanges.

Here's what a section of that looks like:

The emails are not sequential in date and jump by days, months and years, so knowing what was removed from context is simply not possible.

But the results of calculating the differences between the first and last of the numbers in this earlier sequence versus the later sequence is 1.2 million pages, which is the total number of identified gaps from just this one section.

Most of the documents in this section are emails to or from Jeffrey Epstein, including communication with young women who would later accuse him of abuse; email exchanges with his business associates; messages to or from his assistant, Lesley Groff; or emails sent or received by Ghislaine Maxwell.

There is one possible explanation for many of the email gaps. Instructions given to DOJ attorneys working on processing the redactions state:

"If the document is an email chain and the most-inclusive email (i.e., containing all the back-and-forth) has already been reviewed and redacted as appropriate for production, the interstitial back-and-forth can be marked as duplicates."

In other words, all emails exchanged prior to the last email in a chain can be considered a duplicate, because the last one should include all of the messages, and eliminating the duplicates will speed up the redaction process. Once a document is marked as a duplicate, it would likely be excluded from the files.

If that was the case, this was only partially accomplished because duplicate emails still exist throughout the files.

There's also the possibility that errors in the process could have resulted in crucial emails mistakenly being deleted.

The review and redaction process was conducted by hundreds of DOJ attorneys working under a compressed timeline. Given the scale of the task, it's possible that pages were withheld as a result of honest mistakes. But without a roadmap to the redactions and removals, it's impossible to make that determination.

Independent journalist Katie Phang is suing the Justice Department, seeking the release of more files as well as an explanation of redactions and removals. A federal judge has made several rulings in her favor and the DOJ is appealing those rulings.

As part of her lawsuit, Phang is asking the court to appoint a special master to review the files.

"If it wasn't intentional, then was it gross negligence? Were you just lazy? If it was intentional then I think there's [expletive] there that they don't want people to see," Phang told CBS News. "My speculation runs an entire spectrum of reaction — but at the end of the day it just makes the DOJ look bad."

The DOJ has acknowledged making several mistakes.

It admitted to removing, and then restoring, a photo of now Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick on a 2012 visit to Epstein's island , contradicting claims Lutnick had previously made about his contacts with Epstein .

Last year, DOJ officials claimed a minute was missing from prison security video from the night Epstein died, which turned out to not be true .

"This is a case where the process has inhibited public trust in what is ultimately released, and there's a long tradition of this, whether it's the Pentagon Papers or the Epstein files," said attorney Stanley Brand, a veteran litigator and distinguished fellow in law and government at Penn State Dickinson Law.

"This is just another piece where the government process, where making this stuff available just fuels suspicion that there's something we're not seeing, and I don't know that ever gets resolved."

articles.body:
The Hill is thrilled to present the third annual “Bang for Your Buck: Get the Most from Your 2027 Medicare Benefits.”

This year’s event is expanded in scope beyond prescription drug plans to address the most common questions about Medicare during open enrollment, which runs from Oct. 15 to Dec. 7.

Health care costs and affordability are among the top concerns driving Americans’ money worries. For Medicare beneficiaries, and those who care for them, open enrollment is a good time to revisit plans to see whether coverage changed before the 2027 plan year kicks in.

New survey research of Medicare beneficiaries shows major gaps in awareness of newer cost-saving benefits. Results also show the impacts of Medicare negotiation on access and out-of-pocket costs in Part D. The news is mixed.

Additionally, Medicare added 15 Part B drugs to the third round of price negotiations in 2026 and took steps to formalize negotiation policies that could discourage the future development of biosimilars and alternative therapies with improved delivery methods.

Join The Hill, in partnership with the Alliance on Aging Research, for a timely discussion with policymakers, open enrollment experts, and advocates on the future of Medicare benefits, the impact of drug price negotiations, and what beneficiaries need to know for 2027.

The event is scheduled to begin at 8:30 a.m. EDT.

articles.title: Democrats brace for a 2028 presidential free-for-all
articles.summary: The floodgates are about to open in the 2028 presidential race. For the last year, a parade of would-be candidates has quietly — and sometimes unabashedly — tested the waters for a White House bid, traveling to a string of early voting states while meeting with donors and trying out a message with the electorate. Once…
articles.body:
The floodgates are about to open in the 2028 presidential race.

For the last year, a parade of would-be candidates has quietly — and sometimes unabashedly — tested the waters for a White House bid, traveling to a string of early voting states while meeting with donors and trying out a message with the electorate.

Once the midterm elections end in less than a week, the jockeying and positioning will quickly intensify, Democrats say, as potential candidates try to break through in what is expected to be the most crowded field in years.

“It’s going to get hot and heavy real fast,” said Democratic strategist Steve Schale, who helped run former President Obama’s Florida operation during his successful presidential campaigns. “I expect to turn the corner from 2026 to 2028 within the first few weeks after the election because it’s so wide open.”

Democratic strategist Joel Payne, who is also a veteran of several presidential campaigns, put a more definitive time stamp on it: “I’d be surprised if we get to Thanksgiving without some folks putting some stakes in the ground. By Thanksgiving, you’re going to see a lot of the machinery starting to move.”

In the initial weeks, Schale and other Democrats said lesser-known candidates would make their intentions officially known to get a head start with donors and supporters. They’ll also travel to key early states, which the Democratic Party changed in recent months, moving Michigan and New Mexico near the front after South Carolina, Nevada and New Hampshire.

While potential Democratic candidates — including California Gov. Gavin Newsom, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg — can afford to wait before announcing a bid, others need as much time and runway as they can get to build their operations and name recognition.

Democrats predicted that candidates like Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear, Rep. Ro Khanna (Calif.), Sen. Mark Kelly (Ariz.) and former White House chief of staff Rahm Emanuel will begin to push their arguments with their eyes on the Democratic nomination. All of them have been auditioning as they campaigned for midterm candidates. They’ll also begin to meet with Democratic donors and national and local elected officials in the key states to try to shore up support.

On Monday, a CNN report was batted down that Beshear discussed a plan to launch a presidential bid after a meeting of governors in December.

“This is not true,” Eric Hyers, one of Beshear’s longtime allies, wrote on social media.

One Democratic strategist laughed off the “false start” and said the coming weeks would produce more of those moments.

“It’s not true because it’s probably earlier,” the strategist quipped. “Everyone knows Beshear and all these guys want in. And it’s just a matter of when.”

So far, the battle for the Democratic nominee is wide open with no clear front-runner.

A New York Times/Siena poll out last week showed that Harris — who became the 2024 Democratic nominee after then-President Biden stepped away from the race — led the field with 12 percent of Democratic primary voters. Newsom followed with 9 percent, Buttigieg with 7 percent, Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-N.Y.) with 6 percent, Sen. Jon Ossoff (D-Ga.) with 5 percent and Kelly with 3 percent.

Republicans could face a crowded primary of their own. But with the midterms days away, GOP strategists said the outcome would go a long way toward determining the shape of the 2028 field.

For months, the conventional wisdom was that the Republican nomination would come down to a contest between Vice President Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio, egged on in some ways by President Trump, who has made a habit of asking allies about who is better positioned to be the nominee.

But as the midterms inch closer and Republicans brace for potentially significant losses, some party strategists are beginning to envision a larger field.

“If this thing goes as sideways as people are predicting, I think there will be a significant change in direction in 2028. If Vance wants this, he’s going to have to prove that he’s different and that’s going to be a tough hill to climb,” one GOP strategist said. “But I think if things go poorly, there will be an opening for some other candidates to jump in and take over.”

One potential contender is GOP Sen. Ted Cruz (Texas), whom some Republicans expect to enter the race. In recent weeks — as Trump’s polling has cratered — Cruz has appeared to telegraph his ambitions, taking a series of public shots at Vance.

“If anyone thinks the nomination process is going to be an easy one on this side, they’re fooling themselves,” the strategist said.

For now, Democrats have been engaged in early conversations on staffing and fundraising and new strategies on ground game in the early voting states.

The new primary calendar is also driving much of the initial thinking because as Schale put it, “No one has a New Mexico operation and Michigan was always later.”

Democrats are also anxious to redo the disastrous outcome of 2024 and win.

After two years in the wilderness, “people really want to get the conversation started,” Payne said.

articles.title: Trump, Congress set to clash over Hegseth, Iran war, Ukraine after election
articles.summary: President Trump is headed for a showdown with Democrats and members of his party after Election Day over Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s future leadership of the Pentagon, the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war. Democrats are stepping up their demands that Trump fire Hegseth after the midterm elections and warning they won’t support funding…
articles.body:
President Trump is headed for a showdown with Democrats and members of his party after Election Day over Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s future leadership of the Pentagon, the Iran war and the Russia-Ukraine war.

Democrats are stepping up their demands that Trump fire Hegseth after the midterm elections and warning they won’t support funding increases for the Defense Department while the military conflict with Iran is ongoing.

Republicans are warning that Trump will have to push back on Russian President Vladimir Putin and make a stronger commitment to Ukraine if he is to get the Defense funding increases the Pentagon needs after eight months of conflict with Iran.

This sets the stage for a political battle over the Department of Defense (DOD) after Election Day, and some Senate aides warn that if Trump doesn’t give significant ground after Democrats pick up seats in Congress, it could trigger another government shutdown.

“There’s no world in which Democrats are funding the Iran war,” said a senior Senate Democratic aide. “I think Republicans are going to have to do some version of reconciliation if they want to fund the DOD.”

“I don’t know how it plays out if it’s not through reconciliation because I think you’d be hard-pressed to find many, if any, Democrats who are willing to fund it,” the aide added.

Democrats are ramping up pressure on Trump to fire Hegseth after the Nov. 3 election and threatening to impeach him in the next Congress if Trump doesn’t shake up the Pentagon’s leadership.

House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries (N.Y.) is threatening that Democrats will push hard to oust Hegseth if they win control of the House in next week’s elections, as many political handicappers project.

Jeffries is poised to become Speaker in a Democratic-controlled House.

“Pete Hegseth needs to be pushed aside by the president, or we’re going to have to deal with that situation if he is not,” Jeffries told MS NOW over the weekend, suggesting Hegseth could be impeached if he still has his job next year.

Senate Democrats, including members of the Senate Armed Services Committee, have joined calls for Trump to fire Hegseth.

“I think Hegseth should have been fired multiple times,” said Sen. Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.), a member of the Armed Services panel who cited Hegseth’s plan to livestream the execution of Fort Hood mass-shooter Nidal Hasan as the latest reason for ending his tenure.

“The guy has no idea what he’s doing,” Kelly said, adding Hegseth stepping down “would be helpful” to getting the annual Defense authorization bill and the annual Defense appropriations bill on track.

In the House, Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) on Monday indicated in a post on the social platform X that he would reintroduce articles of impeachment against Hegseth when Congress reconvenes in Washington after the election.

Chief Pentagon spokesperson Sean Parnell said Hegseth is focused on his mission of leading and equipping the nation’s armed forces.

“At the War Department, we are solely focused on Peace Through Strength and ensuring our warfighters have everything they need to be successful. We are proud to serve our warriors,” Parnell said, using the Trump administration’s preferred name for the Defense Department.

Pentagon press secretary Kingsley Wilson also defended Hegseth’s record.

“Secretary Hegseth has been a transformative leader for the Department of War. Standards and merit are back, our arsenal is stronger than ever before, and morale and recruitment across every service are at all-time highs. Secretary Hegseth has slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters every step of the way,” the spokesperson said.

Senate Democrats plan to take a hard line against Trump’s request for nearly $70 billion in emergency funding for the department and against the administration’s total request of $1.5 trillion in Defense funding for fiscal 2027.

But Democratic senators are divided over whether the House should impeach Hegseth if they win back control of the lower chamber in the midterm election.

“I don’t think you’re going to see a huge appetite or at least a successful enough vote share to impeach Hegseth in the Senate,” said the Senate Democratic aide, who noted it would require 67 votes in the upper chamber to remove Hegseth from office.

“You’re not f‑‑‑ing getting it, and I don’t think there will be a ton of energy outside of the bunch of folks who are running for president or who are thirsty for clicks to waste time on that,” the source added.

Brian Darling, a GOP strategist and former Senate aide, said Hegseth’s future leadership of the Pentagon will be at the center of an intense partisan fight over funding the department and the rest of government more broadly.

“I think you’ll see quite a bit of pushback” by Democrats against Hegseth and the Defense authorization and funding bills, he said. “That’s a proxy fight over the Iran war, pretty clearly.

“We’ll see Democrats push back pretty hard and they have an opportunity in the lame duck because the CR [continuing resolution] is going to come up and that will be an opportunity,” he added. “If Republicans don’t do well on Election Day, it’s going to empower Democrats to basically take the CR hostage and make demands.”

“And one of those demands will be related to the Iran war and Hegseth’s future,” he added.

Congress needs to pass a CR — a stopgap funding measure — to keep federal departments and agencies operating past Dec. 11.

The prospect of a stalemate over Pentagon funding, which could trigger a broader government shutdown before Christmas, has Senate Republicans discussing the need to push a third budget reconciliation package after Election Day to circumvent a Democratic filibuster in the Senate.

Republicans used a reconciliation package in July of last year to circumvent Democratic opposition to the One Big Beautiful Bill Act and again this year to fund Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol after Democrats objected.

But Republicans are divided over moving both a budget resolution and a follow-up reconciliation process — an arduous and time-consuming process on the Senate floor — given the limited number of legislative days in the lame-duck session.

Sen. Mitch McConnell (R-Ky.), the chair of the Senate Appropriations Subcommittee on Defense, called on Trump in an op-ed published in The Wall Street Journal to work with Republicans and Democrats to pass Defense funding through the regular appropriations process.

But he warned that Trump would need to demonstrate a willingness to get tougher on Putin and make a stronger commitment to Ukraine to get a major funding bill through Congress before Democrats potentially take control of the House, and maybe the Senate, next year.

“Ending the obeisance to Mr. Putin may be table stakes for the end-of-year legislation. The president should plan accordingly,” McConnell wrote.

But Democrats are warning that the Defense spending bills will have a tough time passing after the election even if Trump pledges to take a tougher stance against Russia.

“I think McConnell is too rosy on the opportunity or ability to get funding for the Defense Department,” said the Democratic aide.

articles.title: Senate control is a coin flip — and Democrats’ path runs through Trump Country
articles.summary: With Election Day six days away, Fox News Power Rankings rate Senate control a toss-up as Democrats aim to flip seats in Trump country states.
articles.body: With six days to go until Election Day, the battle for control of the Senate appears to be a jump ball, with the road to the majority running mostly through states President Donald Trump won in 2024. While the final Fox News Power Rankings ahead of the midterms revealed three key shifts in the direction of the Democrats, their hopes of retaking the Senate hinge on flipping seats in so-called Trump Country. As they fight to hold their slim House and Senate majorities, Republicans are fighting political history, as the party in power in Washington has traditionally lost seats during midterm election years. The GOP also faces a challenging political climate fueled by persistent inflation tied in part to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran and Trump's increasingly negative approval ratings. FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: AS IRAN LOOMS LARGE, CAN THE GOP KEEP THE FAITHFUL? The GOP needs to hold 50 seats to retain control of the chamber, since Republican Vice President JD Vance is the tie-breaking vote in the Senate. SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER But if Republicans have a good night and defy expectations, the GOP could hold the majority with up to 52 seats, according to the forecast. articles.title: Recalled butter sold in 10 states receives risk warning: FDA
articles.summary: A popular plant-based butter has been recalled due to yeast, mold and E. coli, and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has now assigned it a risk level.
articles.body:
NEW JERSEY ( WPIX ) — A popular plant-based butter has been recalled due to yeast, mold and E. coli, and the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has now assigned it a risk level .

The recall, which was initiated by Prosperity Organic Foods, Inc., headquartered in Boise, Idaho, involves 1,304 cases of Miyoko’s Creamery European Style Salted Plant Milk Butter.

The FDA assigned the recall as a Class II risk level on Friday, meaning a product may cause “temporary or medically reversible adverse health consequences.” The recall was initially announced Sept. 11.

The affected butter, which is perishable and stored refrigerated or frozen, comes in six-packs of 8-ounce units, which can be identified with the following information:

Lot number and best-by on SBS carton: 07871, Nov. 5, 2026

Lot number and best-by date on the corrugated case for shipment: 1007871, Nov. 5, 2026

The affected products were also sold in Connecticut, Florida, Georgia, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana, Maryland, New Jersey, New Hampshire and Wisconsin.

articles.title: Deep in Trump country, a new generation reveals the divide behind Texas' tight Senate race
articles.summary: Three Texas Tech roommates reveal how abortion rights, oil and gas policy, and cost of living shape their votes in the Paxton-Talarico race.
articles.body: LUBBOCK, Texas — They share a roof, split the bills and attend the same university. But as Texas' unexpectedly competitive Senate race takes center stage in West Texas, three college roommates have very different ideas about who should shape the state's future. The students attend Texas Tech University, where they're balancing classes, career ambitions and newfound independence while navigating political differences that extend far beyond their shared apartment. For Isabella, the election could shape her future career in oil and gas, an industry heavily influenced by government policy. For Kate, women's healthcare and immigration are driving her support for Democrat James Talarico. And for Candy, rising everyday costs and concerns about public education are shaping her vote. Their differences came into focus as President Donald Trump descended on Lubbock to rally alongside Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton on Tuesday. Across town, Democrat James Talarico was courting voters in a state Republicans have dominated for decades. TRUMP WON THIS RELIABLY RED STATE BY DOUBLE DIGITS. NOW A DEADLOCKED RACE IS BRINGING HIM BACK Inside their cozy off-campus apartment, where laptops lie open, notebooks are spread out and favorite snacks are within arm's reach, the three roommates spoke candidly with Fox News Digital about the issues shaping their political views — and how they navigate those differences under one roof. "I don't think we’ll flip anytime soon," Isabella said of Talarico’s bid to turn Texas blue for the first time in more than three decades. Kate, who voted for Talarico, sees things differently. "I think, as a first-time voter, just in general, it's exciting to just feel like you have the ability to make a change," the 19-year-old who hails from Dallas said. The competing perspectives come as the Texas Senate race has become a razor-thin contest, despite Trump's nearly 14-point victory in the state in 2024. A Fox News poll conducted in October found Paxton and Talarico tied at 49% among likely voters, underscoring the unusually competitive contest in a state where Republicans have maintained a firm grip on statewide politics since the 1990s. MEET THE VOTERS WHO COULD BREAK THE GOP’S DECADESLONG GRIP ON A REPUBLICAN STRONGHOLD For Isabella, the election is closely tied to her career ambitions. Studying oil and gas at Texas Tech, she said Republican policies offer a more favorable environment for the energy industry, particularly when it comes to pipeline construction and government regulations. "I don't think that there should be extreme regulations against exploration and production," she said. Kate, meanwhile, said her support for Talarico was driven largely by his positions on abortion and immigration. "I think that women should have the right to their own bodies," she said, expressing opposition to Texas' near-total abortion ban. She also praised Talarico's approach to immigration enforcement, arguing that authorities should prioritize dangerous criminals rather than people working and contributing to their communities. HIGH PRICES PUT TRUMP’S ECONOMY IN THE SPOTLIGHT AS THE GOP FIGHTS TO HOLD CONGRESS Candy, 21, who grew up in Chico, Texas, said she voted for Talarico and Democratic gubernatorial candidate Gina Hinojosa, citing public education, healthcare and affordability. Candy said filling up her car now costs roughly $60 to $70, nearly double the $30 to $35 she previously paid. For a college student already juggling tuition, groceries and other living expenses, that extra cost every week adds up quickly, leaving less room in her budget. "That 30 or 40 [dollars] could go toward other expenses," she explained. Despite supporting Democrats, Candy expressed uncertainty about whether Texas is ready for a broader political shift. "I believe there's hope for Texas, but I don't think Texas is as blue yet," she said. Kate expressed similar uncertainty, saying her experience in a college town has exposed her to more liberal viewpoints than she might not encounter elsewhere in the state. "I hope it flips, but I also am not certain that it'd flip, and it wouldn't surprise me if we didn't flip," Kate said. For Isabella, the prospect of Texas electing a Democrat is considerably less appealing. But despite their competing political views, the roommates have found common ground in an area that sometimes divides people: their shared living space. Navigating those differences isn't always easy. Political disagreements occasionally surface, but the students are learning that difficult conversations can offer opportunities to better understand one another without necessarily changing minds. "I don't think that politics should play a huge role in a friendship or in your living situation," Isabella told Fox News Digital. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Kate expressed a similar sentiment, explaining that she tries to understand her friends as individuals rather than judge them by their political preferences. "My entire personality doesn't change, based off who I vote for," she said. "And their personality doesn't change based off of who they vote for."

articles.title: US midterms: Six days left – who leads in the polls as Trump, Obama rally
articles.summary: Democrats lead national polls as Trump and Obama campaign in key states six days before the US midterm elections.
articles.body:
With six days to go before the November 3 midterm elections in the United States, Democrats are leading Republicans in national polls, but several key Senate races seem too close to call.

President Donald Trump has stepped up his campaigning, holding two Republican rallies in Texas on Tuesday before heading to Ohio on Wednesday. Ex-President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris are also hitting the campaign trail in Georgia for the Democratic Party.

Here is what the latest polls say, what happened on the campaign trail and what to expect on Wednesday.

With less than a week to go before the midterms, a Reuters/Ipsos poll suggests the Democrats are ahead of the Republicans by nine points.

According to the October 22-26 survey, 47 percent of voters support the Democrats, compared with 36 percent who support the Republicans. When undecided voters’ leanings were taken into account, Democrats lead with 50 percent compared with Republicans’ 41 percent.

Trump’s approval rating improved by a percentage point to 32 percent, with 73 percent of US adults saying the cost of living was going in the wrong direction.

In Texas, where Democrats have not won a Senate election since 1988, James Talarico and Republican Ken Paxton are virtually tied in the polls.

Trump has made several trips to the state ahead of the midterms, but the polls indicate a much tighter race than the president has suggested.

“The good people of Texas have probably never seen so much of President Trump. Four visits in seven weeks, which, to put that into context, is twice as many as we saw at the comparable period leading up to the 2024 election, which perhaps shows just how concerned Republicans are,” Al Jazeera’s Phil Lavelle said, reporting from the Texas coastal city of Corpus Christi.

Lavelle said local analysis suggested more Republicans have voted early than Democrats, but Talarico has also been courting Republicans dissatisfied with Trump.

“That doesn’t mean Republicans are voting for Republican candidates,” Lavelle said.

In Michigan , Democrat Abdul El-Sayed and Republican Mike Rogers are also competing in a closely contested Senate race.

“I was a Republican forever, but I became an independent in the last two elections,” Michael Alexander, a Native American backing El-Sayed, told Al Jazeera.

“I don’t really vote for a party any more. I vote for who I think will do the best job.”

Kansas has not elected a Democrat to the Senate since 1932, but Republican incumbent Roger Marshall now faces a close contest against Democrat Adam Hamilton.

The race has brought Trump and his deputy, JD Vance, to the state.

“There’s a reason why we’re seeing not only US President Donald Trump but also Vice President JD Vance heading to Kansas because it’s actually in play,” Al Jazeera’s Patty Culhane said.

According to The Associated Press news agency, both parties and their allied groups have committed about $71m to campaign advertising in the Kansas race, making it the most expensive Senate contest in the state’s history.

What happened in the US midterm campaigns over the past 24 hours?

Trump addressed two campaign rallies in Texas on Tuesday in support of Paxton.

In Corpus Christi, Trump pointed to a tanker that he said was carrying one million barrels of Venezuelan oil and called it a win for his administration. He also suggested the idea of making Venezuela the 51st US state. The Trump administration has signed an oil deal with Venezuela’s interim leader, Delcy Rodriguez, after abducting socialist President Nicolas Maduro in a military operation in January.

Trump also announced plans to roll back the Biden-era restrictions on methane emissions from oil and gas production, stating that it would help bring down energy prices.

Fuel prices have become a huge election issue as the US-Israel war on Iran continues. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also joined Trump for a rare campaign-trail appearance in Texas.

In Alaska, Republican Senator Lisa Murkowski has backed Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins for governor rather than Bernadette Wilson, the Trump-endorsed candidate.

What’s next for Democrats and Republicans on Wednesday?

Trump heads to Ohio on Wednesday for his third rally in the state this month, as Republicans try to defend a Senate seat being challenged by former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown.

The US president is scheduled to speak in Chillicothe at 23:00 GMT. Republican Senator Jon Husted, who took over Vance’s seat when he became vice president, is facing Brown, who is seeking a return to the Senate after losing his seat in 2024.

The two are in a closely contested race, with more than $400m spent or reserved for campaign advertising as of October 8, according to an Axios report.

Republicans are particularly concerned in Texas, Ohio, Kansas and Iowa, where even a few percentage points for a third party could swing the outcome.

Trump is scheduled to hold rallies in Ohio on Wednesday and Iowa on Sunday.

Vance will be in Kinston, North Carolina, campaigning for Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley, who is running against former Democratic Governor Roy Cooper. The vice president is expected to speak at 16:30 GMT.

In Georgia, former President Obama will campaign in Atlanta alongside Democratic Senator Jon Ossoff and gubernatorial candidate Keisha Lance Bottoms at 20:00 GMT.

Ossoff is running against Republican Mike Collins, while Bottoms faces Republican Rick Jackson in the governor’s race. Trump won Georgia in the 2024 presidential election.

Former Vice President Harris also begins a three-day visit to Georgia on Wednesday, with early in-person voting due to end on Friday, October 30.

In Wisconsin, Marquette Law School will publish its latest statewide poll at 18:15 GMT.

Wednesday’s poll will also examine voters’ views on inflation, tariffs, the US-Israel war on Iran and Trump’s presidency.

articles.title: Inside Melania Trump's secret diplomatic role in the Russia-Ukraine ceasefire deal
articles.summary: Melania Trump spent weeks negotiating between Moscow and Kyiv to broker a localized ceasefire in Oleshky, a devastated city in Ukraine's Kherson region.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE: Moscow and Kyiv remain locked in a yearslong grinding war, but in one Ukrainian city, the fight has quieted — and soon the Russian-occupied aging population in Oleshky will be offered humanitarian relief and a way out. Behind the localized ceasefire is an unlikely mediator: first lady Melania Trump. And her diplomatic effort in the war-torn region is not over, Fox News Digital has learned. Trump spent weeks moderating between Russian and Ukrainian officials to hammer out a deal over the devastated city in Ukraine's Kherson region, ultimately winning the trust of both governments to serve as their "exclusive intermediary," according to a senior adviser for the first lady. The agreement brought officials from both countries together in Belarus last week to sign off on a detailed humanitarian operation aimed at getting food, clean water, medicine and doctors into Oleshky, Ukraine, and providing safe passage out for residents who want to leave. Fox News Digital obtained the signature pages of the agreement, signed Oct. 23 by Russia's human rights commissioner, Yana Lantratova, and her Ukrainian counterpart, Dmytro Lubinets. The documents also lay out plans for continued humanitarian operations in the region coordinated with the first lady. For the Slovenia-born first lady, the war in her native Europe was not entirely unfamiliar territory: she had already mediated exchanges of Ukrainian and Russian children. Negotiating an agreement to stop the fighting, however, marked a significant expansion of that role. MELANIA TRUMP'S ADVISOR REVEALS HOW SHE BRIDGED PUTIN, ZELENSKYY TO BROKER FRONTLINE UKRAINE TRUCE Just across the Dnipro from the Ukrainian-held city of Kherson, Oleshky was once home to roughly 24,000 people. Russia seized the city at the outset of its 2022 invasion, and years of occupation and fighting have reduced its population to around 2,000, many of them elderly. The city now sits squarely on the front line. Russian forces use Oleshky as a base for attacks across the river into Kherson, while Ukrainian forces target Russian positions in and around the city. Roads have been mined, food and medicine have become scarce and basic services have largely collapsed. "It's hell there," Yuri Sobolevsky, deputy chairman of the Kherson regional council, told The New York Times. "People need to be evacuated from there, 1,000%. They're living 24/7 under risk of death." For Ukraine, the humanitarian mission presents a difficult tradeoff. The civilians trapped in Oleshky are Ukrainians in desperate need of food, medicine and a safe route out. But the city remains under Russian occupation and sits on an active front line, meaning halting attacks long enough to reach them also means temporarily easing military pressure on Russian forces operating in the area. Getting Russia and Ukraine to stop firing at each other has proven extraordinarily difficult — not just for the first lady, but for her husband and his administration, which has spent much of President Donald Trump's second term trying to bring the war to an end. In Oleshky, however, both sides found a narrow point of agreement. Oleshky first came onto Trump's radar during United Nations General Assembly week in September, when the city's worsening humanitarian crisis was raised at a Fostering the Future Together event that she hosted. By then, the first lady had already worked with both governments to reunify 34 Ukrainian and Russian children with their families across six separate efforts, according to her exclusive senior adviser Marc Beckman, building relationships she was able to leverage when she turned her attention to Oleshky. "The first lady's relationship with both Russia and Ukraine has been, over time, substantial," Beckman told Fox News Digital. "There's a lot of trust, and there's been a lot of success." Her team first approached Ukraine and asked whether Kyiv would authorize Trump to serve as its "exclusive intermediary" with Russia. Ukraine agreed in a formal letter, Beckman said. Trump's team then approached Moscow, and Putin responded with a letter granting her the same role on Russia's behalf. From there, Trump began negotiating with the highest levels of government in Russia and Ukraine, with both Russian President Vladimir Putin and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy involved in the talks, Beckman said. The U.S. side of the negotiating effort was unusually small. Asked how involved the traditional White House national security apparatus was, Beckman said Trump handled the effort. "It's just the first lady," Beckman said. "The devil is in the details," Beckman said of the negotiations. "There were moments in time where things became complicated." What began as an effort to get food, water and medicine to a city on the brink of collapse quickly became an extraordinarily detailed negotiation over how to temporarily stop two armies from fighting. The agreement remains narrowly focused on humanitarian operations in and around Oleshky and does not halt fighting elsewhere in Ukraine, where Russian and Ukrainian forces continue to battle along a sprawling front. RECOVERING FROM LUNG SURGERY, POPE LEO URGES PUTIN TO AGREE TO CEASEFIRE IN RUSSIAN-HELD UKRAINE CITY Trump and Beckman worked through maps, roadways and aerial imagery with the two sides, Beckman said. They negotiated what military equipment could enter the area, how civilians would be evacuated and even arranged refrigerated trucks to recover bodies expected to be found along the way. "We know all of the military equipment that will be brought in," Beckman said. "We even went as far as organizing for refrigerated trucks for the bodies that are going to be there." "It's going to be a very bad scene," he added. "That's the level of detail that the first lady was involved in." The negotiations eventually produced a plan mapped out not just by weeks and days, Beckman said, but by the hour. Russian and Ukrainian officials reconvened in Belarus at 4 a.m. New York time Friday for what was supposed to be a 5 a.m. signing. But negotiations continued for nearly three more hours, with Trump participating by video, before both sides finally agreed to the terms and signed at 7:40 a.m. The ceasefire was initially slated to begin Oct. 29, but the two sides moved the startup by two days, with the guns falling silent at 4 a.m. Moscow time Tuesday. Its geographic scope was also expanded beyond Oleshky to provide safe passage through the surrounding Kherson region for humanitarian convoys. "It was almost like momentum clicked," Beckman said. Russian Gen. Valery Gerasimov, chief of the General Staff, confirmed Russian forces would cease fire along the Kherson axis and facilitate the safe movement of humanitarian convoys into Oleshky. The humanitarian mission itself will be led by civilians from both countries, keeping Russian and Ukrainian troops apart as aid enters the city and residents are evacuated. "If the Ukrainian, the Russian militaries were going throughout Oleshky, they would just kill each other," Beckman said. Four American journalists from Newsmax will also accompany the mission to interview residents and document where they choose to go, providing a record of their decisions as civilians are evacuated from Russian-held territory. The humanitarian mission is expected to last about one week, with a goal of wrapping up in early November. If more time is needed, Beckman said both sides could negotiate an extension with the first lady again participating in the talks. The agreement also envisions a role for Trump beyond the immediate Oleshky operation. Under the terms signed by the two sides, Russia and Ukraine are expected to establish regular humanitarian aid deliveries and repatriation efforts in communities across the Kherson region following the Oleshky mission, with Trump's assistance and coordination. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Those efforts would take place as needed, but at least once a month, according to the agreement.

articles.title: Four investigations Democrats could launch if they win control of Congress
articles.summary: Democrats have promised a wave of probes into the Trump administration if they win back the House.
articles.body:
Democrats in the US Congress are already planning how they would use their power if they win a majority in the House or Senate in next week's midterm elections.

Success is by no means guaranteed, even if midterms can sometimes be brutal for the incumbent party that holds the White House.

Control of the chamber, however, would give the party power to issue subpoenas - summons to testify or produce documents - as well as additional funding to launch investigations early next year.

Democrats are weighing whether to investigate senior figures in the Trump administration - and possibly the president himself. Staffers have begun assembling a list of possible investigations and witnesses, according to people familiar with the discussions.

Here are a few potential Democratic targets if the party emerges victorious on 3 November.

Democrats have made it clear that lucrative deals brokered by the Trump family's vast business empire will be primary targets of any initial investigations.

"We want to make sure that [American] taxpayer dollars are being used wisely and not being stolen or pocketed because of corruption," Virginia Democratic Representative Suhas Subramanyam, a member of the House Oversight Committee, told the BBC.

Items under consideration for investigation include ties between the administration and corporate entities - particularly cryptocurrency firms - as well as the international business dealings of the president's son-in-law, Jared Kushner.

Other topics could include the $400m (£301m) aircraft gifted by Qatar to serve as Air Force One and multimillion-dollar defence contracts awarded to firms linked to the Trump family.

"What's shocking to me is not only that this administration, cabinet officials and even the president and his family have been corrupt and self-dealing, but they've been so brazen and open about it," Subramanyam said.

The White House has repeatedly denied any allegations of wrongdoing.

"President Trump is focused on retaining Republican majorities in Congress and doubling down on the progress he has made to lower costs for families," White House spokesperson Olivia Wales said.

"Democrats have no agenda to improve the lives of the American people, just plans to obstruct and baselessly target President Trump's commonsense agenda," she added.

A White House official said the administration is "always prepared" to respond to oversight requests regardless of who is in Congress.

Democratic lawmakers have vowed to look into Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth's handling of the war with Iran that began in February - including the number of civilian casualties, munitions shortfalls, spending and claims of poorly prepared troops and facilities.

Other topics, according to a source familiar with the discussions, could include boat strikes in the Caribbean that the administration says are aimed at stopping the flow of drugs into the US.

In April, a group of House Democrats filed rare articles of impeachment against Hegseth. They cited the war in Iran and accused him of "high crimes and misdemeanours".

Impeachment requires only a simple majority in the House, but conviction - and removal from office - would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate. No cabinet official has ever been removed this way.

Some experts believe that the negative publicity that would come from congressional hearings could ultimately lead to Hegseth being fired or resigning from the position.

"[If] it looks bad for the White House, and it's a drag on their media attention, President Trump might be likely to cut loose those officials, because he doesn't want that bad press," said David Miller, a political science professor and expert on the presidency at American University in Washington DC. "In a sense that could be a win for the Democrats."

Richard Painter, the former chief White House ethics lawyer under George W Bush, told the BBC that the decision to launch the war should come under scrutiny.

"The bigger issue is this: this war was never authorised by the United States Congress, and I don't care who the secretary of defence is," he said.

"The constitution says that Congress declares war," he said, and lawmakers should "haul these folks in" to answer questions.

In a statement, Pentagon Press Secretary Kingsley Wilson defended Hegseth's record, calling him a "transformative leader" who has "slashed bureaucracy, unleashed innovation, and delivered for our warfighters".

"By every measurable metric, the Department of War is better under Secretary Hegseth's leadership than before," she said, using the administration's preferred name for the defence department.

Senior Democrats - including Robert Garcia, the California Democrat tapped to lead the House Oversight Committee should the party take back the chamber - have identified immigration enforcement as a key priority for potential congressional investigations.

These could examine allegations of misconduct by Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents during immigration raids across the country.

But these investigations may prove difficult and politically tricky.

In 2024, Trump campaigned on a promise of mass deportations of undocumented migrants - a message that resonated with many of his supporters.

But recent polls suggest many Americans, including those who backed Trump in that election, are uncomfortable with some of the tactics used by ICE in American cities so far this year.

It means Democrats will have to walk a fine line between opposing ICE tactics and appearing to dismiss broader immigration concerns, Painter told the BBC.

Democrats are split on the possibility of attempting to impeach Trump for a third time.

Some, such as Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, have expressed support for an impeachment, citing what they view as an unauthorised war with Iran and other alleged impeachable offences.

Others have called for a more cautious approach, arguing that any impeachment is unlikely to end in the Senate voting to remove Trump - who has repeatedly denied any wrongdoing - from office.

It is also unclear whether the party could agree on a reason to launch impeachment proceedings.

"I can do whatever I want, if I want," Trump told reporters in the Oval Office in October, adding that he sees the impeachment efforts in his first term and the later criminal cases brought against him as "very illegal things".

James Comer, the Republican chairman of the House Oversight Committee, told the Washington Sun news outlet in June that Democrats were "one-trick ponies" who were "going to go after Trump".

There is no guarantee for Democrats that any potential investigation would end with a meaningful outcome.

But Subramanyam said their efforts would send a message.

"If we do not do something because we are scared of the optics, or we don't think it will be successful, or they stonewall us, that will be bad," he said. "Not just for the next two years, but for the next 20 years."

articles.title: What’s next for Israel as elections leave no clear winner
articles.summary: In today’s issue: ▪ Uncertainty prevails in Israel elections ▪ Fed’s final rate decision before midterms ▪ CDC deputy director stepping down ▪ Bolsonaro flees Brazil for U.S. As returns are steadily being reported in Israel’s critical parliamentary elections, one thing is becoming clear: there’s uncertainty ahead. The coalition of parties led by Israeli Prime…
articles.body:
▪ Uncertainty prevails in Israel elections

▪ Fed’s final rate decision before midterms

As returns are steadily being reported in Israel’s critical parliamentary elections, one thing is becoming clear: there’s uncertainty ahead.

The coalition of parties led by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu appears on track to finish ahead as of the latest results, currently projected to win 54 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, according to The Times of Israel.

But Netanyahu’s far-right bloc is still expected to fall short of the 61-seat majority needed to form a government, providing an opening for the opposition led by former military chief of staff Gadi Eisenkot .

A retired general who lost both his son and nephew fighting in Gaza against Hamas, Eisenkot is seen as the main alternative for prime minister. His bloc is projected to finish closely behind Netanyahu’s coalition, with 49 seats, as of the latest vote count.

The kingmaker in what comes next may be the two Arab parties — the Joint List and Ra’am — that outperformed expectations and are on track for their best performance ever in Israel’s elections. The parties are currently projected to win as many as 18 or 19 seats, enough to provide or deny a governing coalition.

Joint List chairman Yousef Jabareen told local media that any party seeking to replace Netanyahu’s government will have to engage with his faction. He said he was ready to work to ensure Netanyahu is ousted.

“It is either continued racism, continued exclusion and continued supremacy, or genuine Jewish-Arab partnership,” Jabareen said.

Leading up to the election, Eisenkot dismissed a potential coalition with the Arab parties, but it may be his only path to power.

Voter participation was particularly high, with turnout topping 77 percent, easily surpassing the 70 percent of voters who cast ballots during Israel’s last election in 2022.

Exit polls initially indicated Eisenkot’s bloc would finish slightly ahead of Netanyahu’s, but it’s slipped as votes are counted.

The election has been largely viewed as a referendum on Netanyahu, Israel’s longest-serving prime minister who built his political brand around being the country’s best defender against its many adversaries. That reputation took a hit following the Oct. 7, 2023, Hamas attack, the deadliest incident in Israel’s history.

Netanyahu’s critics have denounced him for failing to stop the attack and point to reports that he was warned in advance but didn’t take action.

One of Eisenkot’s key campaign promises has been to launch an official investigation into what happened surrounding the Oct. 7 attack, which Netanyahu hasn’t allowed. Another key difference between the candidates is the ultra-Orthodox’s exclusion from military and national service, which Eisenkot has pushed to end.

Netanyahu and Eisenkot don’t differ significantly on the issue of the offensives against Hamas and the Iran-backed Hezbollah in Lebanon. Both are also hawkish on Iran. The Hill’s Laura Kelly reports that Israel’s foreign policy is likely to remain stable regardless of who comes out on top.

Once all the votes are tallied, the responsibility will fall to Israeli President Isaac Herzog to choose the party he views as having the best chance at forming a government through coalition negotiations. Even though Netanyahu’s party is on track to be the largest in the Knesset, Herzog doesn’t have to choose Likud.

The party leader chosen will have 28 days to form a coalition, with a possible 14-day extension. If those negotiations fail, Herzog can turn to another party leader with the same 28-day timeline.

The final formation of Israel’s government could take weeks. And if no party is able to form a governing coalition, another election could be on Israel’s horizon.

“Change” was a common refrain among voters who spoke to Kelly, who is reporting from Israel this week. She has a breakdown here on the situation with the election too close to call.

▪ The Jerusalem Post : Party leader urges opposition to unite with Arab parties.

▪ The New York Times : Herzog faces a difficult choice.

You are going to start to see breakdowns in the coming days on how many Democrats and Republicans are turning out across the country. One thing, however, we’ve been following is how independent voters will shape this election. I spoke with Andrew Yang about Matthew McConaughey’s recent viral video , and he said this might not be the last time you hear from the actor.

“The speculation has officially been stoked, and you don’t put out that kind of video if you’re not thinking about it,” Yang said of McConaughey’s potential political future.

Here’s one reason why I bring this up: Yes, the midterms are six days away, and the attention is fully on Tuesday. However, the 2028 speculation will further hit overdrive mere hours later.

Burman hosts “The Hill” weeknights, 6 p.m. EDT/5 p.m. CDT on NewsNation.

A federal grand jury has rejected the Justice Department’s (DOJ) attempt to charge former White House aide Cassidy Hutchinson over her testimony to Congress about the President Trump’s conduct during the Jan. 6, 2021, Capitol attack. This marks the latest incidence of a grand jury refusing to hand up an indictment that the DOJ requests, a rarity that has become more common during the second Trump administration.

Trump said he will ban the term artificial intelligence (AI) from “all relevant documents, and everything else,” in favor of the term super intelligence (SI). He signed an executive order last month directing the executive branch to use SI, instead of AI.

The leaders of Finland and Norway initiated a direct call with Russian President Vladimir Putin amid broader efforts to wind down the war in Ukraine. They made clear they spoke only on behalf of their countries, but some European leaders criticized them for breaking with the rest of Europe.

Federal Reserve Board Chairman Kevin Warsh speaks during a news conference at the Federal Reserve in Washington, Sept. 16, 2026. (Mark Schiefelbein, Associated Press)

HOLD STEADY : The Federal Reserve will announce its latest interest rate decision today, in one of the last major pieces of economic news ahead of the midterm elections Tuesday.

The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) is widely expected to hold its benchmark rate steady at 3.75 percent to 4 percent, though another rate hike is expected before the end of the year. The Fed raised rates by a quarter of a percentage point last month for the first time since 2023.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh is opposed to sharing any forward guidance on rate decisions, but CME FedWatch, which relies on 30-day Fed funds futures prices, puts the likelihood of a hold today at more than 90 percent and the likelihood of a rate hike at the next meeting, scheduled for Dec. 8-9, at more than 75 percent.

Affordability and cost of living concerns have been a central focus of the midterms. Annual inflation climbed to 3.7 percent in September, according to the consumer price index, with rising gas prices accounting for more than half of the monthly increase.

▪ The Hill : Fed likely to hold rates steady ahead of midterms.

▪ The Hill : Consumer sentiment ticked up in October after 10-year low last month.

ROLLBACK :The Trump administration announced a proposed rule to scrap regulations on methane emissions from the oil and gas sector. Trump touted the proposal at a rally in Texas last night.

The draft rule would particularly ease regulations on “marginal wells,” which produce just 7 percent of the nation’s oil and gas but account for roughly half of its methane emissions. Methane is responsible for about 25 percent of global warming, and it’s 28 times as potent as carbon dioxide.

The administration expects the rollback to save the oil and gas sector $45 billion and allow for an additional 210 million barrels of oil production and 1.41 trillion cubic feet of natural gas from 2027 to 2050. The Hill’s Rachel Frazin reports that the U.S. consumes roughly 21 million barrels of oil and 92 billion cubic feet of natural gas each day, so the additional production would account for about 10 days’ worth of oil and 15 days’ worth of gas.

▪ The Hill : Dems urge Trump to restore climate funds in goodwill gesture.

QUICK STINT: Jennifer Shuford , the deputy director and chief medical officer of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), announced Tuesday that she will leave her job just four months after Trump appointed her to help steady the agency.

Shuford, a former Texas health commissioner, will stay on through Nov. 12, the CDC said. Her departure comes as the agency faces scrutiny for its handling of measles outbreaks around the country and refusal to accept Pennsylvania’s reported measles-related death count.

In a statement, Shuford said she is leaving to spend more time with family, and she thanked Trump and Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. for “giving me the opportunity to help lead the CDC,” saying, “It has been an amazing experience and I will be forever grateful for it.”

▪ The Hill : Senate Dems press insurers on Trump’s ObamaCare coverage cuts.

▪ The Hill Insider : Trump officials say men face testosterone crisis. Experts respond.

BAD TIMING : The Federal Election Commission’s (FEC) electronic filing system has been down for hours as the agency’s IT staff works to restore the service, a spokesperson confirmed to The Hill’s Miranda Nazzaro .

It was not immediately clear what caused the outage, but Reuters reported that the FEC website was targeted by a hacker or hackers.

The FEC’s incident update page first indicated that the agency was investigating the issue Monday night, and said “a fix is being implemented” as of this morning. The FEC’s website search function for campaign donations, recipients and political action committee information did not appear to be affected by the outage.

The FEC’s functions should not impact the electoral process next week.

▪ The Hill : CFTC sues Utah over efforts to block prediction markets.

▪ The Hill : Kalshi adds protections for users 18 to 20 years old.

The president will receive an intelligence briefing at 11 a.m. He will greet the Artemis III crew at 1:30 p.m. He will travel to Chillicothe, Ohio, to deliver remarks at 7 p.m. and then return to the White House.

President Trump points to supporters during a campaign rally, Oct. 27, 2026, in Corpus Christi, Texas. (Eric Vryn, Associated Press)

GETTING READY : Democrats are preparing for the Trump administration to attempt to interfere in the results of the midterms following a series of remarks from the president and actions targeting various states.

The Department of Justice’s (DOJ) preemptive lawsuit filed last week to challenge the results of the Alaska Senate race if Sen. Dan Sullivan (R) loses reelection spurred of post-election meddling. The DOJ argues a win by former Rep. Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) could be the result of confusion with fellow candidate Daniel J. Sullivan on the ballot.

Peltola asked a federal judge to dismiss the case , arguing it’s “baseless” and amounts to an illegal attempt by the federal government to wade into the election.

Trump has also directed his attention at Minnesota, writing in a post on Truth Social that his administration is “watching closely” for voter fraud in the Senate race.

That comes after the DOJ earlier this month gave California election officials 48 hours to set aside 20,000 ballots the department claimed were from noncitizens and on Monday asking officials in Washington state to review a list of more than 400 registered voters it believes could be noncitizens.

The Hill’s Julia Manchester reports that these efforts have sparked fears among Democrats that the administration might challenge the results if Republicans take big losses on Election Day.

“If and when the election deniers in the Trump administration try similar or new tactics this fall, we will be ready to fight back and ensure that the results are certified according to the will of the voters,” Rachel Jacobs, a senior partner at the Democratic-aligned Elias Law Group, told The Hill.

When asked if he would respect the midterm results , Trump said Tuesday that he would “if they’re honest elections.”

▪ The Hill : Vice President Vance responds to question about ‘insulting’ Alaska lawsuit.

▪ The Hill : What to know a week out from the election.

Opposition presidential candidate Sen. Flavio Bolsonaro speaks after the presidential runoff in Brasilia, Brazil, Oct. 25, 2026. (Eraldo Peres, Associated Press)

WHERE IN THE WORLD : Following his surprise defeat in Brazil’s presidential election, right-wing Sen. Flávio Bolsonaro has reportedly fled his country to travel to the U.S. as he faces an investigation into allegations he committed financial crimes.

Multiple outlets reported that Bolsonaro, who lost a hotly contested runoff election to Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva on Sunday, left Brazil through Argentina en route to the U.S. A senior State Department official told The Hill that the department will issue visas to Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the country.

Brazilian Supreme Court Justice Alexandre de Moraes ordered Bolsonaro to surrender his passports shortly after the election and barred him from leaving the country. The senator has been under investigation for alleged involvement in a money laundering scheme.

Bolsonaro’s brother, Eduardo , publicly urged him to leave Brazil if he lost the election. A deadline for him to surrender his regular and diplomatic passports passed at noon Tuesday.

He acknowledged the order in an Instagram video Monday as he went to meet with his father, former President Jair Bolsonaro . The younger Bolsonaro’s loss is a blow also to the former president, who is under house arrest as part of his prison sentence following his conviction for his role in the Jan. 8, 2023, attacks in the Brazilian capital Brasilia.

Jair Bolsonaro and others convicted of crimes related to the attacks were expected to receive a pardon if Flávio Bolsonaro won.

The younger Bolsonaro had seemed to be on the precipice of being elected president of South America’s largest country after he finished first in the first round of Brazil’s presidential election earlier this month. But Lula managed to pull off an impressive comeback to win another four-year term in the head-to-head runoff.

Flávio Bolsonaro rejected the results and called for the election to be annulled over a court order keeping the polls open for two hours longer on election day, which was made at both candidates’ requests. The senator’s party recognized the results Monday, even as Flávio Bolsonaro has not conceded.

▪ Axios : Brazil’s election ignites MAGA’s midterm warnings.

▪ The Associated Press : Environmentalists celebrate Lula’s reelection.

Justice for Camp Lejeune families cannot depend on an election , Rep. Mark Takano (D-Calif.) writes in The Hill.

The ‘weapon of war’ argument has backfired on AR-15 bans , Matthew Cavedon writes in The Hill.

Sophia Bush speaks on a panel during the Global Citizen NOW summit, May 14, 2026, in New York. (Heather Khalifa, Associated Press)

And finally … The Hill’s “In the Know” columnist Judy Kurtz sat down with “One Tree Hill” actress Sophia Bush yesterday to discuss her political activism and why she doesn’t feel the need to limit herself to just entertainment.

“What would I do, silence myself? Take away one of my most important rights to be more palatable or more hirable to people I don’t know? That’s not something that I’m interested in,” Bush told Kurtz , when asked about her decision to campaign in 2008 for then-Democratic presidential nominee Sen. Barack Obama (Ill.).

Bush shared details of her life in the entertainment world and in politics in a wide-ranging conversation about her new book, “And I Will Tell You Mine.”

“You have stories you’re finally ready to tell, and I think for me, after years of advocating for other people and for community, it felt really special to turn that patient attention inward and actually decide to share some things about my own personal individual life,” she said.

articles.title: Ballots in the hallway: How California can restore lagging faith in our elections
articles.summary: California can end this argument without proving that anyone cheated. It has to lock the ballots, verify the rolls and publish the results of both.
articles.body:
Hundreds of mail ballots sat piled in an open hallway at a Skid Row shelter this month, according to a California Post investigation . Reporters said they authenticated a photo and confirmed the scene on October 13 at the Midnight Mission, where 1,160 voters are registered .

The mission says its policy is “locked doors.” A hallway, last I checked, lacks doors. California can end this argument without proving that anyone cheated — it must lock down the ballots, verify the rolls and publish the results of both.

The asset at risk here is confidence. A University of California-San Diego survey of 11,400 eligible voters found that only 60 percent expect votes to be counted accurately nationwide in the midterms, down from 77 percent right after the 2024 election. The loss of confidence is bipartisan, among Republicans, Democrats and independents alike. Some of my liberal friends who previously held as an article of faith that it is blasphemy to question election results. Now they too are asking, “Who checks the checkers?”

Skid Row has a record here. In 2018, Los Angeles prosecutors charged nine people in a scheme that offered homeless residents $1 or a cigarette to forge petition and registration signatures. In 2020, four people pleaded no contest and received probation or suspended sentences.

In May, federal prosecutors charged a Marina del Rey petition circulator with paying someone to register to vote, and she agreed to plead guilty . Prosecutors say she gave homeless registrants her former address, which would have sent their ballots to a home where they had never lived. Who would cast them?

How many people get away with such schemes without being indicted?

In September, a federal grand jury indicted a Victorville man and two others, alleging they used stolen voter identities to fill initiative petitions on Skid Row. The Victorville defendants are presumed innocent. In June, the FBI confirmed “investigative activity” there after videos circulated in which residents described being paid to register to vote or sign ballot petitions. Those videos remain unverified.

This year’s mayor’s race had more plot twists than Breaking Bad. On election night, Spencer Pratt, a former reality TV personality, led Councilmember Nithya Raman by more than 40,000 votes. But as mail ballots were collected, they reversed the count. Raman advanced to a runoff with Mayor Karen Bass, 29 percent to Pratt’s 26 percent . The county certified the results on June 26, 24 days after the election had taken place.

Add Proposition 50, the extreme gerrymander that voters approved in November 2025 with 64 percent to turn five Republican-held districts over to Democrats , and one-party control hands the skeptics plenty of material.

A fair reading of the Midnight Mission report is limited. Nobody has shown those ballots were stolen or altered. Los Angeles’ top federal prosecutor, Bill Essayli, confirmed an investigation into Skid Row ballots but declined to say whether it covers the mission.

Shelters can be lawful registration addresses, and a county spokesman cautioned that registration records do not show who lives where. The mission says it has 296 beds, with about 125 more people sleeping in its dining room or courtyard. Those points answer fraud accusations but leave the hallway unexplained.

Marcus Aurelius wrote , “If it is not true, do not say it.” The rule binds activists who shout fraud without evidence, but also officials who insist everything is fine.

The dispute is now in federal court. The Justice Department asked a judge to make California set aside the ballots of about 20,000 registrants it calls likely noncitizens until their citizenship is verified. California disputes the list, and Judge Gabriel Sanchez pressed the department’s lawyers on how it was compiled.

Prosecutors also announced election-crime charges against 28 alleged noncitizens. A Los Angeles County assistant registrar told the court the office has no independent way to verify citizenship beyond what voters attest, and Gov. Gavin Newsom’s (D) office replied that California follows federal law. On Monday, a divided Ninth Circuit panel rejected the emergency request , two-to-one, ruling only on procedure. At argument, dissenting Judge Patrick Bumatay said that without an injunction “you will never know.”

California takes pride in being a sanctuary state for illegal immigrants. Its sanctuary law , which the Ninth Circuit upheld in 2019, limits state and local help with federal immigration enforcement. In my view, that posture makes Sacramento slow to welcome federal help verifying citizenship, even though the state already uses the federal SAVE program for some benefits, including Medi-Cal.

Three fixes require nobody to assume anyone cheated. California can check voter rolls against SAVE or an equivalent citizenship database before ballots go out. It can set written custody rules for organizations that receive ballots for residents, with locked storage, signed logs and spot audits. Third, it can publish registration counts by facility address and audit the outliers, starting with the Midnight Mission. Ballots deserve at least the security of the snack shack key at a Little League field.

Louis Brandeis, years before joining the Supreme Court, offered the remedy : “Sunlight is said to be the best of disinfectants.” With Election Day less than a week away, Ronald Reagan’s old advice still fits: “Trust, but verify .”

Jay Rogers is a financial professional with more than 30 years of experience in private equity, private credit, hedge funds, and wealth management.
