articles.title: China encroaches dangerously close to US land as a single ship breakdown exposes major vulnerability
articles.summary: A single mechanical failure on Coast Guard Cutter Healy halved U.S. icebreaking capability as four Chinese research vessels operated near Alaska.
articles.body: America's ability to maintain a presence in the Arctic remains thin enough that a single mechanical failure cut the Coast Guard's icebreaking capability in the region in half this summer. And the breakdown comes as Chinese vessels are expanding their activity around Alaska. Rear Adm. Bob Little, commander of the Coast Guard's Arctic District, told Fox News Digital the failure of Coast Guard Cutter Healy left him with just one of two icebreakers that had been slated to operate in the ice. Meanwhile, four Chinese research vessels were operating in the region. "Healy's unexpected mechanical failure cut in half my capability to operate up in the ice," Little said. ARCTIC POWER PLAY GIVES TOP US ADVERSARY NEW OPENING WITH RUSSIA AS US STAKES GROW The shortfall comes as the U.S. faces a growing need to maintain a presence in waters that can take days to reach. Chinese research vessels are gaining experience in the Arctic and collecting data that can also have military applications, including for submarine operations, while Russia's much larger icebreaker fleet gives Moscow greater ability to move ships and supplies through the region. The Coast Guard is now racing to add ships, aircraft and surveillance capabilities as shrinking sea ice opens more of the Arctic to navigation. But its next generation of icebreakers is still years away. "I can't get those icebreakers soon enough, given the operational environment," Little said. Little said nearly $25 billion in recent funding will support 11 new Arctic Security Cutters, with the first expected to arrive in the region as early as 2028. The buildup comes as the Coast Guard's operating area is effectively growing. Declining sea ice is opening more navigable water around Alaska, bringing more commercial and military activity into areas that were once harder to reach. "As that new operational area becomes accessible, we see an increase in human activity for economic development, for military advancement," Little said. "And that activity is creating a need for additional Coast Guard mission." China has become an increasingly regular presence in those waters. Little said Chinese research activity has grown from as few as one vessel appearing episodically in the Arctic to five last year, while four operated there this year. Those vessels are not necessarily violating international rules. The Coast Guard Cutter Munro recently returned from a 112-day Arctic patrol that included monitoring Chinese research ships, and Little said the Coast Guard did not observe activity on the surface that fell outside customary law or international norms. RUSSIA PULLED BACK FROM THE ARCTIC, FOR NOW. NATO MUST ACT BEFORE THOSE TROOPS RETURN The concern, he said, is what China can learn simply by operating there. "Any research vessel that operates in the Arctic has the ability to conduct both scientific research," Little said. "It could be economic research that could be for future exploitation of critical minerals and scarce resources." "And then all of that research helps aid in military activity if you're trying to identify seabed floors and navigate subsurface assets," he added. Troy Bouffard, director of the Center for Arctic Security and Resilience at the University of Alaska Fairbanks, said China's research activity gives Beijing experience operating in an environment where it has historically had little. "They're pretty desperate to gain operational experience and knowledge in terms of their growing military capabilities," Bouffard told Fox News Digital. The research vessels collect legitimate scientific data, he said, but that information can have other applications, "especially when it comes to submarine warfare planning." For the U.S., Bouffard said the challenge is about more than the number of icebreakers. Unlike the North Atlantic, where the U.S. and its allies have decades of infrastructure and experience, the North Pacific side of the Arctic has far less infrastructure to support a sustained presence. "If we can't have presence, surface presence in an area, it's very difficult to manage issues that may escalate," Bouffard said. The distances compound the problem. Getting a ship from Kodiak, Anchorage or Seattle into the Bering Sea can take several days, Bouffard said. Russia already holds a substantial advantage in its ability to maintain access through its much larger icebreaker fleet. "Advantage certainly falls in their favor," Little said. Russia's fleet allows it to maintain access, sea lanes and logistical routes for commercial and military purposes, he said. "Certainly, as we look at the military advantage, there is a need for the United States to keep up and to ensure that we have ice presence and ice capability," Little said. The Coast Guard is also watching cooperation between Moscow and Beijing. Little said the service has observed joint Russian-Chinese military surface groups, cooperation between their coast guard forces and Chinese research vessels collaborating with Russia and "likely sharing information." "But anytime they're working together, we're watching closely to see if they pose any threat to homeland security or a military risk to the United States."

articles.title: Poll shows Hochul adding to lead over Blakeman in New York governor's race: 'Running out of time'
articles.summary: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul leads Bruce Blakeman by 14 points in a Siena poll, but a plurality of voters say neither will make life more affordable.
articles.body: New York Gov. Kathy Hochul expanded her lead over Republican challenger Bruce Blakeman to double digits in a new poll showing the Democratic incumbent pulling further ahead in the final days before Election Day. Hochul leads the Nassau County executive 54% to 40% among likely New York voters, according to a Siena Research Institute survey released Wednesday. The 14-point margin is five points wider than her lead in September, when she led 50% to 41%. "Heading into the final stretch, Hochul has a 14-point lead, with Blakeman quickly running out of time to close a gap that is growing rather than narrowing," Siena pollster Steven Greenberg said in a statement. NEW YORK GOVERNOR DEBATE HEATS UP AS BLAKEMAN, HOCHUL SPAR OVER TRUMP, SANCTUARY STATUS, ICE SHOOTING The poll also showed Blakeman struggling to establish an advantage in areas where Republicans typically need strong support to compete statewide. The candidates are virtually tied in upstate New York and the downstate suburbs, while Hochul leads independent voters by 11 points. Republicans generally need strong margins in those regions and among independents to overcome Democrats' roughly two-to-one voter registration advantage and their dominance in New York City, Greenberg noted. "But with only a week to go, Blakeman and Hochul are running virtually evenly upstate and in the downstate suburbs, while Hochul has an 11-point lead with independents," Greenberg said, noting that Blakeman is "quickly running out of time to close a gap that is growing rather than narrowing." Despite Hochul's overall advantage, the survey revealed uncertainty among voters over whether either candidate would make life more affordable for average New Yorkers. DEBRA MESSING SAYS COST OF LIVING, SUBWAY VIOLENCE PUSHED HER TO BACK TRUMP-ENDORSED REPUBLICAN A plurality of voters, 35%, said neither candidate would make life more affordable, compared with 30% who chose Hochul and 27% who selected Blakeman. Hochul also reached a new milestone in the survey, with 51% of likely voters viewing her favorably compared with 45% who viewed her unfavorably. It marked the first time a majority of voters had viewed her favorably in Siena polling during her five years as governor. Her job approval rating also rose to 51%, up from 48% in September. Blakeman, meanwhile, received a 39% favorable rating and a 40% unfavorable rating. The survey found a sizable gender gap, with Hochul leading Blakeman by 23 points among women and six points among men. She also led among Black voters, 81% to 16%, while White voters were closely divided. The poll also found that 68% of likely voters believed Hochul would win the election, compared with 23% who predicted a Blakeman victory. Among Republicans surveyed, 40% said they expected Hochul to win. In New York's other statewide races, Democratic Attorney General Letitia James led Republican Saritha Komatireddy 54% to 39%, while Democratic state Comptroller Tom DiNapoli led Republican Joseph Hernandez 59% to 32%. The Siena poll was conducted Oct. 19–22 among 807 likely New York voters through telephone and text-to-web surveys. It has a margin of error of plus or minus 4.1 percentage points. articles.title: The midterm legal fight is already here
articles.summary: Lawyers are bracing for next week’s midterm elections to land in court. But already, battles over California ballots and an Alaska Senate candidate are heated. articles.body:
Lawyers are bracing for next week’s midterm elections to land in court.

But already, battles over California ballots and an Alaska Senate candidate are heated.

In California, the Trump administration alleges the state sent 20,000 likely noncitizens mail ballots and is facilitating illegal voting by refusing to verify them.

U.S. District Judge David Carter is expected to rule today on whether to set the ballots aside after an appeals court declined to do so. At a Tuesday afternoon hearing, it didn’t sound good for the Justice Department. Carter suggested the government should instead prosecute any individuals it’s concerned about.

“We’re busy,” U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli joked at Tuesday’s hearing. Earlier this month, federal prosecutors charged 28 foreign nationals with election crimes in California.

“Well, we’ll get you busier,” retorted Carter, an appointee of former President Clinton.

Lawyers on both sides have agreed it’s not feasible to segregate ballots once they’re processed — hundreds of thousands are already in — and a noncitizen’s vote that’s able to get through would ultimately be counted.

But California insists it has no obligation to verify voters’ citizenship merely because of the Trump administration’s accusations. The state also argues it’s not practical so close to Election Day.

“I would ask the state, how many illegal votes is OK for them? Is it five? Is it 10?” Essayli pushed back.

Groups like the NAACP are backing the state, saying that accepting the Trump administration’s position would be a monumental shift.

Anna Baldwin , director of voting rights litigation at the Campaign Legal Center, which represents the NAACP in the case, said on Tuesday it opens “Pandora’s box.”

“The consequence of that is chaos. It is confusion,” she said.

What to watch for when Carter rules today: Even if the judge refuses to immediately set aside the ballots, he signaled he may order an expedited hearing over the next two weeks to get more testimony and information about the government’s claims.

Meanwhile in Alaska, U.S District Judge Sharon Gleason is fast-tracking the Trump administration’s case over the two Dan Sullivans on the ballot.

One is the incumbent Republican who has served in the Senate since 2015. The other is a man named Daniel J. Sullivan, who Republicans argue sought to confuse voters by seeking access to the ballot under the same name.

The Justice Department is suing, and Gleason wants all the written arguments in hand by the time the clock strikes noon in Anchorage on Friday (4 p.m. EDT). Then, the appointee of former President Obama is expected to decide whether to toss the suit.

The Alaska Supreme Court ruled in June that both Sullivans could remain on the ballot.

It now lists “Dan S. Sullivan,” with a note indicating his status as the incumbent and a registered Republican. The other man is listed as “Daniel J. Sullivan Jr.,” with no added context.

That brings us to a what might some call a preemptive legal challenge by the Trump administration.

On Thursday, the Justice Department filed a lawsuit seeking to block the certification of Alaska’s Senate results if the senator loses his reelection bid, namely to Democrat Mary Peltola .

They argued that the tally should not be certified until an investigation determines whether any votes for Dan J. Sullivan were meant to go to the incumbent.

“Should Alaska certify any electoral results tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J. Sullivan … the State and its officers will fail in its obligation to protect the integrity of its election,” DOJ attorneys wrote.

Peltola’s campaign wants to dismiss the case, calling it a “wholly baseless” challenge. Democrats argued in court filings that the Justice Department has no authority to intervene in how a state runs its election.

The two cases have led to plenty of speculation of what’s to come. But election law experts see it nothing more than an experiment of gaming out the worst-case scenario.

“OK, doomer,” read the headline of a Boston Globe opinion piece by Notre Dame Law School professor Derek Muller , a widely recognized election law scholar.

To Muller and others, many of Trump’s efforts are doomed to fail once tested by a court of law.

“There is a fine line between vigilance and panic. The last weeks of this 2026 election cycle are testing that line,” Muller wrote in a blog post.

Still, it may be a while before the dust settles.

Specifically, set your calendars for when the new Congress is seated on Jan. 3.

The Constitution provides that each chamber “shall be the Judge of the Elections, Returns and Qualifications of its own Members.”

Our colleague Alexander Bolton reports that in the Senate, lawmakers are bracing for a potential floor fight over seating the winner in Alaska if Republicans lose. Dive deeper here.

Most senators aren’t up for reelection this year. So let’s focus on the House, which starts anew come Jan. 3. Even if the GOP holds onto its majority, Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) will have to be voted back into the role. Everything starts over.

The Speaker election is nearly the first thing on the agenda, but not quite. Beforehand, the House clerk will announce the election certificates received from the states, which indicate the winners who will assume each seat.

It’s a role held by Kevin McCumber , who has been in the job since 2023. He’s been working in the clerk’s office on and off for three decades, including stints during Rep. Nancy Pelosi ’s (D-Calif.) time as Speaker.

The hypothetical goes like this: Should the GOP maintain its majority, the Speaker just before noon Jan. 3 fires McCumber and tries to bring in an official in his place, who refuses to seat Democrats, and things get messy. That hypothetical scenario was pushed into the national spotlight this summer, particularly by legal pundit Jeffrey Toobin, who in an opinion piece for The New York Times described it as the “worst thing” Trump could do in the midterms. Some election law experts have cast it aside.

“As a matter of positive law, I do not think this scenario is viable,” Matthew Seligman , a fellow at Stanford Law School’s Constitutional Law Center, wrote in July about the suggestion.

Beaver’s: Travel center giant Buc-ee’s is suing Beaver’s Mini Mart in Beavercreek, Ohio, for trademark infringement over allegations that the small retailer’s cartoon beaver mascot is too similar to their own. The store claims it has used the same branding for decades and never heard an objection from Buc- ees until the lawsuit was filed. Read more from our colleagues at Nexstar affiliate WDTN .

Our colleagues at Nexstar affiliate KTLA dug into the lawsuit .

Anthropic officially registered for its widely anticipated IPO this week.

As investors parse the newly unveiled S-1 filing for details about the AI company’s revenue growth and corporate structure, it also includes nearly 100 pages disclosing potential business risks. It provides a glimpse into the legal frontiers that lie ahead.

To start with, the company has faced lawsuits from book publishers, the music industry and media outlets alleging it has violated federal copyright law. In July, a judge approved Anthropic’s $1.5 billion settlement with authors in a lawsuit concerning thousands of books.

Those cases raise an untested question: How do authors’ legal protections apply when AI models are trained using their work?

“An adverse ruling against us or another company in our industry could result in injunctive relief that restricts our ability to use or distribute models trained on the data at issue or could require us to retrain affected models from scratch at substantial cost,” Anthropic warned in its filing.

Then, there’s potential litigation over accusations that AI models are harming children. State attorneys general have launched lawsuits against other Big Tech companies in recent years over similar claims, with cases sometimes resulting in massive sums.

The list goes on. Anthropic warns that courts may not take kindly to the fact that it doesn’t retain prompts, and some plaintiffs allege the company’s efforts to slow down the development of AI alongside other industry players violate antitrust law.

There’s also the issue of what legal framework governs when an autonomous AI model makes decisions. Can Anthropic’s Claude chatbot enter a binding legal agreement on behalf of a user?

“We may face claims from customers, their end users, or third parties alleging that we are liable for harm caused by our agents’ autonomous actions, even where the customer configured, deployed, or supervised the agent. The absence of settled legal standards creates significant uncertainty,” Anthropic wrote in its filing.

Some of Anthropic’s legal risks aren’t unique to AI.

It entered a standoff with the Pentagon earlier this year for refusing to allow its Claude model to be used in fully autonomous lethal weapons or for the mass surveillance of Americans. The Pentagon designated Anthropic a supply chain risk, and the company filed two lawsuits. It won one filed in California but has lost the other, brought in the nation’s capital. Both remain ongoing.

“While we continue to work with government agencies, we cannot be certain that the resolution of these lawsuits will not adversely affect our ability to sell to government agencies and other customers that sell products and services to the U.S. government,” Anthropic’s new filing reads.

But amid all the uncertainties, you can count on one normal strategy: Anthropic is making Delaware the exclusive forum for shareholders that want to launch securities lawsuits down the road.

Testimony from FBI Special Agent Bryan Witt is expected to continue as a federal judge in D.C. weighs whether there is probable cause to charge two former FBI officials with lying to Congress in the probe of Hunter Biden’s laptop.

Mohammed Sabry Soliman , who has pleaded not guilty to federal hate crime charges in connection with a Molotov cocktail attack at a Boulder, Colo., rally for Israeli hostages last year, may change his plea at a hearing in Denver. The attack killed one person and injured a dozen others.

A status conference will be held in D.C. for Cole Thomas Allen , the man accused of attempting to assassinate President Trump at the White House Correspondents’ Association dinner, in which a trial date may be set.

Former Cleveland Guardians players Luis Leandro Ortiz Ribera and Emmanuel Clase de la Cruz are expected to appear for a pretrial conference in Brooklyn, N.Y., on charges related to their alleged roles in a sports betting scheme.

A federal judge in D.C. will hold a hearing to weigh former FBI Director James Comey’s motion to dismiss charges against him for allegedly disclosing sensitive national defense information in October 2016.

The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments in Maxwell v. Thomas , a case concerning the scope of prisoners’ habeas petitions, and Younge v. Fulton County Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, a civil procedure dispute stemming from when the office fired its No. 3 official.

The Supreme Court will hear oral arguments in St. Mary’s Catholic Parish v. Roy , a case examining whether Colorado can exclude faith-based preschools who do not want to admit LGBTQ families from universal preschool program funding.

articles.title: Watchdog accuses DSA candidate of blurring charity, business and campaign: ‘What happened to all that money?’
articles.summary: The NLPC complaint alleges Angie Nixon's Moxie Group nonprofit left $210,000 in spending unaccounted for as she campaigns for Florida Senate.
articles.body: The National Legal and Policy Center (NLPC), a conservative government watchdog, filed a complaint on Monday against Angie Nixon, a state legislator and candidate for U.S. Senate in Florida backed by the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA), alleging that she may have violated "a number of Florida and federal laws." The complaint asks authorities to probe whether she used her now-defunct nonprofit, the Moxie Group Inc., to benefit herself. It comes as Nixon wages an uphill race to unseat Sen. Ashley Moody, R-Fla. Nixon's campaign disputes the characterizations, noting that Nixon's involvement with the nonprofit ended in December 2025 when she resigned as its principal manager. The Moxie Group was initially intended to receive federal tax-exempt contributions for a community project named Café Resistance, a community-oriented bookstore and coffee shop in Jacksonville. NLPC is asking the Federal Election Commission, the IRS, the U.S. Attorney’s Office and the Florida attorney general to investigate the Moxie Group along four lines: unaccounted-for charitable expenses, overlap between the nonprofit and a for-profit business, whether it solicited donations even after the group was disbanded and whether Nixon’s use of her business space for campaign purposes violates federal campaign restrictions. DEFEATED PROGRESSIVE ‘SQUAD’ LAWMAKER IN HOT SEAT FOR NON-PROFIT’S MISSING PAPER TRAIL According to the Moxie Group’s 2024 reporting, it spent $210,000 with an "other" designation, leaving most of its spending unaccounted for. "While she itemized some of the charity’s expenses … a whopping $210,000 ... was simply listed as ‘other’ with no description or itemization of what those funds were spent for even though the form requires the charity to ‘list item’ for those ‘other’ expenses. What happened to all that money?" NLPC wrote in its complaint. Parts of the $210,000 figure have broad descriptions but lack itemization in the 2024 reporting. Two of them under the "other" designation include one $42,560 payment and another $68,304 disbursement, both under "program services." A third, a $3,437 item, is categorized under "management & general." Outside the "other" category, listed expenses include equipment rentals, insurance, advertising, information technology and fees for non-employees. The unknowns in the money trail, NLPC contends, are especially important given the overlap between Nixon’s nonprofit and her business — the complaint’s second area of concern. The document notes that after founding her nonprofit in 2019, Nixon transferred its registration license to her personal for-profit company by the same name — DBA Café Resistance Bookstore and Coffee Shop. SENATE HOPEFUL'S 'TREADING WATER' NARRATIVE CRUMBLES UNDER $500K CAMPAIGN PAYOUTS TO FAMILY "Although the charity was ostensibly established to raise funds for a local community bookstore/café, the license for that establishment was transferred to her for-profit The Moxie Group LLC DBA Café Resistance Bookstore and Coffee Shop," the complaint reads. Third, NLPC questioned whether Nixon raised donations for her nonprofit even after its board of directors voted to disband the group on Dec. 15, 2025. "It waited over nine months to file Articles of Dissolution with the Florida Secretary of State on Oct. 1, 2026," the group wrote. The complaint says the Moxie Group did not take down its fundraising site, stating that its contributors were promised "a tax receipt for making a donation," a confirmation for charitable donations. The complaint includes screenshots of the now-archived website. Fox News Digital is not aware of any specific contributions the Moxie Group may have received that were directed to the nonprofit during that time. Nixon's campaign noted that, because she stepped down as the nonprofit's manager in December 2025 — ahead of the board's disbandment on Dec. 15 — she would not have been involved in any decisions about the group's articles of dissolution or donations received after her resignation. As its final area of concern, NLPC believes that previously reported accounts of letting the group use its space for campaign events — without some form of payment — would constitute a violation of campaign finance laws. "It appears that the Café Resistance and Bookstore has been functioning as the candidate’s campaign de facto headquarters or a branch thereof. Indeed, Café Resistance is hosting a phone bank operation on its premises," the complaint states. According to Nixon’s campaign website, the coffee shop is listed as the location for "Ten toes down Tuesday phonebank," an event scheduled for Tuesday, Oct. 27. "Let’s go all in for Angie!! Tuesdays can be so fun when we spend them phonebanking for Angie! Together we will call registered voters to remind them that early voting is going on statewide and we need them to vote, now more than ever! Bring your charged-up phone, laptops and/or tablets!" the event’s description reads. Nixon’s campaign said it has not made payments to Café Resistance and has used only the group’s parking lot. The campaign also noted that Nixon does not own the building. Even so, NLPC also noted that if any of the funding that had been made as a contribution to the nonprofit had ended up paying for the business’ rent, that could also constitute a campaign finance violation, the group contends. SENATE REPUBLICAN SETTLES SIX-YEAR-OLD CAMPAIGN BILL AFTER BEING CALLED OUT ON SOCIAL MEDIA "To the extent that contributions to the charity were used to pay the rent and expenses of the for-profit Café Resistance Bookstore and Coffee Shop, which in turn was used for Angie Nixon’s political campaign, that is a clear violation of 501(c)(3) rules that prohibit charities from using their funds for political campaign purposes," the document reads. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Having secured the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate earlier this year, Nixon will face off against Moody next week in the state's Nov. 3 general election.

articles.title: LEE CARTER: America is angry at everyone — but who will actually vote?
articles.summary: Democrats lead midterm election polls, but the gap narrows sharply among voters certain to participate, making voter turnout the key factor.
articles.body: America is furious. Democrats are furious at Trump. Republicans are furious at Democrats. Independents are furious at just about everyone. At last, something we can agree on. INDEPENDENT VOTERS AREN’T PICKING A POLITICAL TEAM, THEY JUST FEEL PICKED ON With just under a week until the midterms, Americans are being told that everything is at stake. Democracy. The economy. Our freedoms. The future of the country itself. And yet, according to AP-NORC polling, only about two in 10 voters believe either political party is strongly focused on helping people like them or capable of solving important problems. We've never been told an election matters more. We've rarely expected less from the people we're electing. So here's the question I've been thinking about as a pollster. LEE CARTER: THE SUMMER POLLS MISSED THE POINT: VOTERS ARE MOVING — AND THE MIDTERMS BEGIN What happens when everyone is angry, but not everyone is angry enough to vote? Because that's what makes this election so difficult to predict. We spend an enormous amount of time asking Americans whom they support. But in a midterm election, the more important question may be whether they care enough to show up. And the latest polling suggests those are two very different things. TRUMP VOTERS REVEAL THEIR BIGGEST FEAR HEADING INTO MIDTERMS — AND IT'S NOT RISING PRICES A CNBC survey found that 74% of Democrats worry President Donald Trump will exceed his constitutional authority if Republicans retain control of Congress. Meanwhile, 54% of Republicans fear Democrats will enact democratic socialist policies. Those aren't equivalent concerns, or equally intense ones. But they tell us something important about the electorate. Democrats fear a president with too much power. Republicans fear a government with too much reach. Both sides have plenty to be angry about. DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS BUILDING. HERE ARE 3 FORCES THAT COULD STOP IT But anger doesn't vote. People do. And here's where things get interesting. Research examining the 2018 midterms found that worry helped predict who actually voted. Enthusiasm did not show the same relationship. Remember 2018? Nearly half of eligible Americans voted, the highest midterm turnout in more than a century. Apparently, Americans don't necessarily need to love their candidates to get themselves to the polls. Sometimes worrying about the alternative is motivation enough. Which brings us to 2026. Pew Research finds Democrats have a substantial motivation advantage. Among voters who say they're extremely motivated, Democrats lead Republicans by 24 points. If those were the only people voting, Democrats could start planning a very enjoyable election night. But look at a different group. Among people who actually voted in both 2022 and 2024, the Democratic advantage is just six points. That's an enormous difference. The people who say they're most motivated to vote aren't necessarily the same people with the strongest history of showing up. And that's a distinction worth remembering before anyone starts declaring a landslide. The latest Fox News poll gives Democrats a 54% to 45% advantage on the generic congressional ballot. But among voters certain to participate, that lead narrows to six points. CBS News projects Democrats will win 229 House seats, enough to reclaim the majority. But CBS has identified another complication. Democrats have more voters who say they're definitely voting or have already voted. Republicans have more voters who say they might vote. In other words, Democrats have more of the voters who say they're coming. Republicans have more of the voters who haven't decided whether to bother. And that may be the most important political question of the next week. Will those Republicans show up? Will they stay home? Will something happen in the final days that convinces them this election matters? Nobody knows for certain. And in a closely divided House, the answer could determine who controls Congress. This is why polling is both enormously useful and endlessly frustrating. We can measure what Americans think with considerable precision. Predicting what they'll actually do is harder. In fact, one of the most revealing findings from Pew's analysis of the 2022 midterms is that Republican gains were driven largely by differences in turnout, not a great wave of voters changing their minds. Among Americans who voted in both 2020 and 2022, very few switched parties. What changed was who showed up. Seventy-one percent of Trump's 2020 voters participated in the 2022 midterms, compared with 67% of Biden's 2020 voters. Four points. Not exactly the stuff of dramatic campaign commercials. But across millions of voters, a few points can change the outcome of an election. Sometimes elections aren't decided because Americans change their minds. They're decided because different Americans show up. And suddenly, a few things about this campaign begin to make more sense. Take Trump's whistle-stop tour. Why is a sitting president spending the final days of a midterm campaign racing from rally to rally when his approval ratings are so low? Because Republicans may not need him to change many minds. They need him to get the right people out of the house. Trump has demonstrated an unusual ability to attract voters who don't always participate in elections. The challenge for Republicans is getting those voters to show up when Trump himself isn't on the ballot. A rally may not change someone's opinion of the president. But it might change whether that person votes. And in a close election, that's worth considerably more than another favorable headline. Then consider something that has received surprisingly little attention: voter registration. Since 2018, the party-registration balance has shifted toward Republicans by roughly eight points in North Carolina, seven in Pennsylvania, five in Nevada and four in Arizona. Those aren't election results. Registering Republican doesn't mean someone will vote Republican, and it certainly doesn't guarantee they'll vote at all. But the shifts suggest the pool of potential voters has changed. And that matters enormously when turnout is the great unknown. Democrats may have an advantage among voters who say they're highly motivated. Republicans may have a larger reservoir of potential voters than older assumptions about the electorate would suggest. The question is whether those voters show up. Registration tells us who's on the roster. Polling tells us who's ahead. Turnout tells us who actually plays. That's why a few points of registration movement, a presidential rally and the enthusiasm gap are all pieces of the same story. And it's why the outcome remains so difficult to predict. Now consider the mood of the country. The latest Fox News poll finds that 74% rate the economy negatively. Sixty-six percent are dissatisfied with the direction of the country. Just 18% say their families are better off than two years ago. Americans are unhappy. That's clear. But unhappiness doesn't automatically tell us what they'll do. Some angry voters become activists. Some become reliable voters. Some decide the whole system is hopeless and stop paying attention. The same emotion can produce very different behavior. And there's another complication. Americans aren't particularly convinced that voting will solve their problems. An October AP-NORC survey found roughly eight in 10 registered voters want Congress to prioritize lowering the cost of living. Yet CBS finds that most voters don't expect their financial circumstances to improve regardless of which party wins. Americans know exactly what they want fixed. They just don't have much confidence that either party will fix it. That creates two competing forces. Fear of what happens if the other side wins may drive people to the polls. But frustration with both parties may convince some voters that the outcome won't make much difference. Which force wins? That's the question. And the parties are spending an extraordinary amount of money trying to influence the answer. Since Sept. 1, Democrats have spent more than $163 million on advertisements mentioning Trump. Republicans have spent approximately $11 million doing the same. Democrats are spending nearly 15 times as much talking about Trump as Republicans are. Apparently, Democrats have decided their most effective campaign spokesman is Donald Trump. Republicans seem considerably less enthusiastic about putting him in their advertisements. But all that advertising is ultimately aimed at the same objective. Get people to care enough to vote. Early voting is already running ahead of the comparable point in 2022. More than 13 million early and mail ballots had been cast nationally by Oct. 22, compared with roughly 9 million at a similar point four years ago. That sounds like a sign of enormous enthusiasm. Maybe it is. Or maybe people who would have voted on Election Day are simply voting earlier. Early voting tells us that ballots are being cast. It doesn't necessarily tell us how many additional people will vote. And it certainly doesn't tell us which party will benefit. The same is true of outrage. A country can be furious and still produce a surprisingly close election. A party can dominate among the most motivated voters and still struggle if the other side's less enthusiastic supporters decide to participate. And a candidate can win without persuading many people who weren't already inclined to vote for that candidate. That's what makes this election so difficult to predict. The most important voters may not be the ones changing their minds about Democrats or Republicans. They may be the ones changing their minds about whether to bother voting at all. Of course, the polls currently favor Democrats. The Fox News survey gives them a meaningful advantage. CBS projects they will reclaim the House. Those are important findings, and they shouldn't be dismissed. But a poll is a picture of an electorate. An election is an event in which some of those people participate and others don't. The difference can be decisive. So as we head into the final week, I'd pay less attention to the loudest voices and more attention to the people we aren't hearing from. The occasional voter. The dissatisfied independent. The Republican who dislikes the direction of the country but isn't sure the Democrats would be better. The Democrat who fears Trump but isn't convinced Congress can change much. These are the people who could decide the election. Not necessarily because they've changed their minds about politics. But because they may change their minds about participating. The swing voter who changes parties gets all the attention. But the voter who swings between voting and staying home may decide this election. And that's why Trump is on the road. Democrats are spending millions talking about him, and both parties are fighting over people who already agree with them. The question isn't just which party Americans prefer. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP It's which party can get its Americans to vote.

articles.title: Leftist streamer triggers fury after mocking 'funny' injuries to ICE agents at Ilhan Omar event: ‘Disgusting’
articles.summary: Hasan Piker mocked injured ICE agents during a Minneapolis campaign event with Rep. Ilhan Omar, drawing swift condemnation from conservatives.
articles.body: Far-left streamer Hasan Piker sparked online controversy after he mocked the Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents injured in Operation Metro Surge during a campaign event alongside Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., Monday night. Recalling his time in Minnesota amid protests over the Trump administration’s federal immigration crackdown, Piker said he thought agents must be "extra racist" to be out in frigid winter temperatures and mocked one of them who was injured as the crowd laughed along. "We saw a lot of funny compilations as well, you know. A lot of hip bones were broken. 'Officer Martinez down,'" he said while speaking to Democratic socialist and failed Minneapolis mayoral candidate Omar Fateh, who hosted the sold-out Minneapolis event. Piker has joined several prominent Democrats on their campaign trails, emerging as a polarizing figure within the Democratic Party that some are embracing while others are rejecting. He has made national headlines for past rhetoric, including his claim that "America deserved 9/11," and has faced accusations of antisemitism over his remarks on Israel and Hamas. ILHAN OMAR'S RADICAL STREAMER ALLY RALLIES WITH EMBATTLED LAWMAKER AFTER DC HOME RAID Omar, who shared the stage with Piker that night, has been immersed in controversy of her own after Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) agents searched her Washington, D.C., home earlier this month and a federal court filing identified the congresswoman as "Ilhan Nur Said Elmi, aka Ilhan Abdullahi Omar." Rep. Angie Craig, D-Minn., and Sen. Amy Klobuchar, D-Minn., publicly condemned Piker, while other Minnesota Democrats called for the event to be canceled as voters prepare to head to the polls ahead of next week’s midterm elections. Omar’s campaign backed her decision to attend to mobilize young voters. Piker also told Fateh that he was inspired by the "solidarity" and "mutual aid" following the deployment of thousands of ICE and Customs and Border Protection agents to Minnesota. Protests resulted in multiple arrests, objects and fireworks thrown at law enforcement and the disruption of a church service. Two U.S. citizens, Renee Good and Alex Pretti, were killed during interactions with federal law enforcement. ILHAN OMAR JOINS 'POLARIZING AND DANGEROUS' STREAMER AT CAMPAIGN EVENT DESPITE DEMOCRATIC BACKLASH "It wasn’t just the networks that were very quickly propped up, the mutual aid that I saw, the protests that sparked up that said, ‘We’re not going to take it. We’re not going to sit aside and watch this administration come and rip our communities apart and kidnap our neighbors,'" he said. Piker, who streams his commentary on Twitch, called Republicans "terrorists" during the event, and Omar referred to the party as the "pedophile protection party." Conservatives on social media quickly condemned Piker's comments. "Hasan Piker was asked what stuck with him from Operation Metro Surge in Minneapolis: ‘Funny compilations’ of federal agents being injured," Charlie Kirk Show executive producer Andrew Kolvet posted on X. "He also called the agents ‘extra racist.’ This isn’t comedy. It’s tacit support for the far-left insurrection network against federal law enforcement. Pro-revolution. Pro-anarchy." "Every Democrat he campaigned with should be asked if they agree. Disgusting." "Hasan and his elected Democrats are sick," Loomer Unleashed posted on X. HASAN PIKER LASHES OUT AT REPUBLICANS, CALLS THEM 'TERRORISTS' IN EVENT WITH ILHAN OMAR In another post on X, Crucible Updates wrote, "Hasan watched federal agents get hurt and his takeaway was 'funny compilations… a lot of hip bones were broken.' Millions of young women take their politics from this guy. Let that sink in." "WTF?!" Gina Milan, a conservative media personality, posted on X. "This guy is America’s biggest cancer. Just another Nepo baby," Kevin Smith, host of Loud Majority Live, posted on X. A Department of Homeland Security (DHS) spokesperson said in a statement to Fox News Digital that the "vilification" of ICE agents who "put their lives on the line" every day to enforce the law is contributing to a more than 1,600% increase in assaults against them. "They should be thanking our law enforcement for removing these dangerous criminals from Minnesota—NOT vilifying law enforcement," the spokesperson wrote. "While these people smear ICE, law enforcement is arresting criminals and saving countless American lives." The spokesperson added that ICE agents do not target individuals based on skin color and take required steps to determine immigration status and removability before making an arrest. "Politicians and activists must turn the temperature down and tone down their rhetoric," the spokesperson wrote. Omar is running against former state trooper John Nagel and independent candidate DeVelle Jackson in the upcoming midterm elections for Minnesota’s 5th Congressional District. articles.title: Thune calls Ohio race 'ground zero' in 'knife fight' for Senate while rallying with Husted
articles.summary: John Thune called Ohio "ground zero" for Senate control, warning that a Democratic majority could lead to a 24-month Trump impeachment trial.
articles.body: Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., called Ohio "ground zero" for Senate control during a campaign event with Republican nominee Sen. Jon Husted in Lima, Ohio, on Tuesday night. Following remarks from Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services Administrator Dr. Mehmet Oz, Thune praised Oz's work in rooting out waste, fraud and abuse while insisting that Republicans must hold a Senate majority to allow Oz to continue his work. "That only happens if Jon Husted gets elected next Tuesday. This is ground zero. It seems like it is a lot of election years we come to Ohio, but this literally is ground zero. This is the firewall in the United States Senate. It's the difference between the next two years, President Trump having to deal with Democrats in Congress, House and Senate, where all you'll be doing is investigations," Thune told the crowd. SENATE CONTROL IS A COIN FLIP — AND DEMOCRATS’ PATH RUNS THROUGH TRUMP COUNTRY Top Democrats, including House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries, D-N.Y., and Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., have already signaled an intention to use subpoena power to investigate President Donald Trump and members of his Cabinet. "When people ask what will we do, my answer is simple. We'll use those tools. We'll act like the Congress," Meeks, the ranking member of the House Foreign Affairs Committee, told the Associated Press in September. HOUSE DEMS PLOT TRUMP INVESTIGATION BLITZ IF THEY SEIZE MAJORITY "I tell people that the first thing the House will do, Democrats, if the House flips, is they'll impeach the president," Thune continued Tuesday. "Well, that will require a trial, some sort of a trial in the United States Senate. And the only difference between a 24-hour impeachment trial in the Senate and a 24-month impeachment trial is a Republican majority," he said. DEM MAKING SENATE COMEBACK BID SAYS HE WOULDN'T SUPPORT A TRUMP IMPEACHMENT PUSH Thune then slammed Husted's Democratic opponent, former Sen. Sherrod Brown, who served as a U.S. senator in Ohio from 2007 until 2025, when he ceded his seat to Republican Bernie Moreno after losing in the 2024 election. "He proved that to us for 30 years when he was in the Senate, he was a rubber stamp for Chuck Schumer and Nancy Pelosi and Joe Biden. We got to keep Jon Husted in the United States Senate, folks. It is absolutely, absolutely critical," Thune said. SHERROD BROWN'S 1971 LETTER ARGUED AGAINST RELEASING VIETNAM WAR POWS, PODCAST HOSTS REVEAL Thune continued to sing Husted's praises. "Jon Husted is as good as they come. He is just a solid, solid human being who is principled, hardworking, smart and solution-oriented. He's getting up every day thinking of things he can do to make Ohio better. He did that when he was here in the state legislature and as lieutenant governor for the state of Ohio. He cut taxes here. Came to Washington, cut taxes there. Allowed you to keep more money in your pocket. Secured the border. We haven't had a person released into the country illegally in 17 months. Think about that, folks," Thune continued. TRUMP ADMIN MARKS 15 STRAIGHT MONTHS WITH ZERO BORDER RELEASES AS APPREHENSIONS PLUNGE 94% He closed his remarks by hammering home how crucial it is for Ohioans to get out and vote. "This is a knife fight, folks. This is a bare knuckles brawl, and all you have to do is turn on your television and see that. But the stakes couldn't be higher, consequences couldn't be greater. It's just so important that we get this done," he concluded. MAPPED: THE STATES TRUMP AND TOP DEMOCRATS ARE TARGETING BEFORE ELECTION DAY Husted, for his part, reiterated the tight nature of his race, also challenging Republican voters to get to the polls. "We got work to do because this is going to be a close race. This is going to be a close race," Husted told the crowd. "This is like the fourth quarter of a football game. I can tell you that the other side wants to intimidate us. The other side wants to make you think that we're not going to win. The other side is going to try to make you believe that what you do doesn't matter. What you do does matter. You get into the fourth quarter of a football game, and this is what people try to do. They try to intimidate you the whole game. Everybody has a game plan, but they keep punching you. They keep knocking you down. They want to make you quit. Are they going to make you quit?" FOX NEWS POLL: ECONOMIC ANXIETY AND CANDIDATE CONCERNS DEFINE OHIO SENATE RACE A recent Fox News survey of likely Ohio voters showed Brown with a slight lead over Husted, with 52% of respondents saying they'd vote for Brown compared to 47% for Husted. articles.title: Mike Collins drops Election Day gas price prediction in heated Georgia Senate race
articles.summary: Republican Rep. Mike Collins details his private conversation with President Trump after the Perry rally and his role in landing Audi's $4.2 billion deal.
articles.body: EXCLUSIVE — Republican Rep. Mike Collins offered a behind-the-scenes look at his latest conversation with President Donald Trump and detailed his role in preparing Georgia's infrastructure for a multibillion-dollar manufacturing investment during an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital on Tuesday, exactly one week before voters decide one of the nation's closely watched Senate contests. Collins, a trucking company owner challenging Democrat Sen. Jon Ossoff, said he spoke privately with Trump following Saturday's rally in Perry, Georgia, where the president announced a $4.2 billion investment by German automaker Audi. The Georgia congressman described a president eager to hear feedback from those around him and said he personally relayed what he had observed while meeting rallygoers. TRUMP SUPPORTERS CONFRONT IRAN, AFFORDABILITY CONCERNS WITH A MESSAGE FOR CRITICS: 'GIVE HIM TIME' "He always wants to know what you think. He wants to know what everybody thinks," Collins told Fox News Digital. "And I think that's just part of his personality." Collins said he made a point of asking attendees whether they had ever been to a Trump rally before. "Well over half of the people that were at that event, it was their first time ever attending a Trump rally," Collins said, describing his own conversations with supporters. The Republican also revealed that Trump helped amplify a new digital advertisement from his Senate campaign focused on the Laken Riley Act, legislation Collins championed in Congress. TRUMP-BACKED CANDIDATE SURVIVES GRUELING RUNOFF, ADVANCES TO HIGH-STAKES SENATE RACE "When he saw the ad, he retweeted it out there and of course, it has exploded with over 7 million views," Collins said. The president's involvement comes as Collins seeks to unseat Ossoff in the final days before the Nov. 3 election. Collins also elaborated on his involvement in improvements to the Port of Brunswick, which he credits with helping position Georgia to attract Audi's newly announced manufacturing investment. Trump announced Saturday that Audi would invest $4.2 billion in a new facility in the Macon area, with plans to manufacture approximately 200,000 vehicles annually. Collins said that after becoming chairman of the House Water Resources and Environment Subcommittee in 2025, he made the Port of Brunswick one of his first priorities. "Got down there and, lo and behold, that thing has not been fully dredged in over 10 years," Collins said. "Took me about three months, got the money, got it dredged. Now it is fully dredged." According to Collins, insufficient channel depth had limited what cargo vessels could transport through the port. He argued that improving the port's capacity helped make Georgia more attractive to automakers looking to manufacture and export vehicles. "One of the reasons that they picked Georgia was because that port is ready to go down there," Collins said. ‘MISLEADING VOTERS’: OSSOFF WARNS DONORS HE’S FALLING BEHIND DESPITE LEADING SENATE FUNDRAISING The Audi announcement has become a point of contention in the Senate campaign. Ossoff has called for more details about the project, while Collins has pointed to his work on port infrastructure as evidence of his economic development record. The interview also turned personal when Collins was asked about reports concerning Ossoff's campaign spending on a Hollywood makeup artist. The Washington Times reported Sept. 26 that Ossoff's campaign had spent nearly $3,000 on hair and makeup during the election cycle, more than any other Senate candidate at the time. The outlet cited Federal Election Commission records showing payments to Georgia makeup artist Stephanie Ponder. Asked whether he personally wears makeup on the campaign trail, Collins responded with a joke. "The answer is no, I don't use makeup," Collins said. "Some people might want to suggest I put a bag over my head." Collins then said political advisors had deliberately changed how Ossoff looks and speaks. "I can't help it that they hired Pee-wee Herman's makeup artist," Collins said. The comments followed Trump's own references to the fictional character while criticizing Ossoff at Saturday's rally. Collins also claimed that Ossoff is positioning himself for a potential 2028 presidential campaign, an allegation he framed as his own interpretation of the senator's voting record, endorsements and fundraising. Ossoff has campaigned on his work in the Senate, including healthcare, affordability and economic issues, while criticizing Collins' support for Trump's policies. When asked whether he disagrees with Trump on any issue, Collins pointed to the timing of a potential change involving off-road diesel fuel. "Probably the only thing I would have, I would have jumped on the off-road diesel quicker to run in trucks," Collins said. The trucking company owner argued that allowing additional diesel supplies into the transportation market sooner could help reduce prices. He also predicted that consumers would see lower fuel prices following the election. "You're gonna see prices come down. It's amazing what Election Day is gonna do," Collins said. The prediction comes as rising energy costs remain a major issue in the Senate race. Collins defended Trump's broader economic agenda, arguing that lower taxes, deregulation and domestic manufacturing investment would help households struggling with everyday expenses. Ossoff, meanwhile, has criticized Trump's tariffs and the economic effects of the war with Iran, arguing that administration policies have contributed to higher costs for Georgia families. Collins ended the exclusive interview with a confident declaration about the approaching election. "I'm gonna win this race next week. I'm gonna be your next U.S. senator from Georgia," Collins said. He added that he would move his work from the House to the Senate while continuing to focus on affordability and economic development. "We're gonna just pick up that old desk, move it across the rotunda, and continue to deliver," Collins said. articles.title: Trump's unusual legal gambit against Biden-era deportation rule pays off at Supreme Court
articles.summary: The Supreme Court allowed a Texas-DOJ agreement ending the Biden-era administrative closure rule that let judges delay deportation proceedings.
articles.body: The Supreme Court, with no noted dissents, has allowed an agreement between Texas and the Department of Justice ending a Biden-era immigration rule to go into effect. The Biden administration adopted the rule in 2024, formally establishing procedures for immigration judges to temporarily pause certain deportation proceedings through a practice known as "administrative closure," including when migrants were pursuing immigration relief through other federal proceedings. The Supreme Court's move leaves in place a lower court ruling eliminating that rule, stripping away a procedure that allowed certain deportation cases to be put on hold. Texas sued the federal government in June, arguing that the rule was adopted without proper legal authority. The Department of Justice agreed with Texas, asking the judge overseeing the case to vacate the rule and prevent similar rules from being adopted in the future. JUDGE WHO APOLOGIZED TO ACCUSED WOULD-BE TRUMP ASSASSIN LIGHTS UP DOJ IN HUNTER BIDEN FBI CASE Opponents accused Texas and the Justice Department of colluding to eliminate the Biden-era rule, arguing that the two sides worked together despite being on opposite sides of the lawsuit. On the same day the DOJ made its request, District Judge Reed O’Connor, an appointee of President George W. Bush, granted it. TRUMP-APPOINTED JUDGE SLAMS DOOR ON DOJ AS COURT LOSSES PILE UP DAYS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS' In August, however, three cities with large immigrant populations — Baltimore, Maryland; New Haven, Connecticut; and Columbus, Ohio — joined with Centro Legal de la Raza, an immigrant legal advocacy group, in an effort to intervene in the case and defend the Biden-era rule on appeal. The cities argued that eliminating the rule could lead to residents being deported, reducing their tax revenues and giving them legal standing to challenge the agreement. O’Connor rejected that argument. MAMDANI BLASTS FEDS FOR WAGING 'CAMPAIGN OF VIOLENCE AND TERROR' AGAINST NYC'S IMMIGRANTS On Oct. 9, the three cities and Centro Legal de la Raza asked the Supreme Court to temporarily block the lower court's judgment while their appeal proceeded, accusing Texas and the federal government of engaging in "egregious collusion" to eliminate the Biden-era rule. Federal lawyers argued that the cities and their allies lacked legal standing to challenge the agreement because they had not demonstrated the concrete injury required for a federal court to consider their claims. CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP "We are deeply disappointed that the Supreme Court declined to intervene to prevent the Trump-Vance administration from dismantling longstanding immigration court procedures through a backdoor agreement with Texas," the cities and Centro Legal de la Raza said in a statement shared with Fox News Digital. "For decades, these procedures have allowed immigration judges to temporarily pause deportation proceedings for people pursuing lawful immigration relief, including survivors of violence, abused and neglected children, and victims and witnesses who cooperate with law enforcement," the statement continued. "Eliminating these protections puts vulnerable people at greater risk of deportation and undermines public safety in communities across the country."

articles.title: Talarico rally warmup act calls for abolishing ICE, contrasting Senate hopeful's message
articles.summary: Malik Williams called to abolish ICE and legalize cannabis at a James Talarico rally, despite Talarico's recent denial of supporting that policy.
articles.body: Malik Williams, a Democratic candidate for a seat in Texas' state legislature, called for abolishing Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) and for legalizing marijuana during a Tuesday rally for U.S. Senate nominee James Talarico in Lubbock, Texas. "We can legalize and tax THC and cannabis. We're gonna abolish ICE, we're gonna tax the rich and we're going to get my friend, the next United States senator from the state of Texas, James Talarico, elected!" During a joint CNN and Jubilee town hall, Talarico directly denied wanting to abolish ICE when asked if he supported the idea. JAMES TALARICO TORCHES BIDEN BORDER POLICIES IN STUNNING ATTACK AD AS PROGRESSIVE TRIES TO FLIP TEXAS BLUE "No, and I never have," Talarico responded, adding, "We need Immigration and Customs Enforcement in this country, but that's not what we're seeing. EXCLUSIVE: RESURFACED VIDEO SHOWS JAMES TALARICO DISCUSSING ‘EXCITING’ OPPORTUNITY TO END ‘OVER-POLICING’ Talarico's recent remarks, however, depart from past comments. ICE executed a man in broad daylight on our streets just this morning. It's time to tear down this secret police force and replace it with an agency that actually is going to focus on public safety," he said. FOX NEWS POLL: MAJORITY SAYS IMMIGRATION ENFORCEMENT HAS CROSSED THE LINE Talarico also advocated for "hauling in" agents in front of Congress to testify on actions taken during enforcement actions. Abolishing ICE is an unpopular opinion among Republicans nationwide, with 67% strongly opposing the idea, according to a July YouGov/The Economist poll. The same poll found 48% of Americans overall supporting ICE's abolition. TRUMP WON THIS RELIABLY RED STATE BY DOUBLE DIGITS. NOW A DEADLOCKED RACE IS BRINGING HIM BACK Texas voters, meanwhile, have a moderately negative view of the agency as a whole. Only 42% of the state views the agency as very favorable or somewhat favorable, compared to 47% of the state viewing ICE as somewhat unfavorable or very unfavorable, according to a February poll from The Texas Politics Project. In introducing Talarico on Tuesday, Williams also stumped for a wide number of policies popular with the rising crop of democratic socialists while appearing to bash President Donald Trump and Talarico's Republican opponent Ken Paxton. DEMOCRATS CAN TAKE THE LEAD ON ONE OF THE NATION’S TOP ISSUES – DATA CENTERS "When we have embarrassing loser representatives that support a fascist, racist, rapist, war criminal, I say we deserve better! When the backbone of Texas, our ranchers and farmers, tell us that they do not want data centers and then our politicians, as they love to do, they force it upon us without consent, I say we deserve better!" Williams exclaimed to fanfare. The Williams and Paxton campaigns did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital for further comment. The Talarico campaign pointed Fox News Digital to his comments from the CNN town hall.

articles.title: China exile-turned-GOP nominee warns socialist surge could give Beijing greater influence in Washington
articles.summary: Lily Tang Williams, a New Hampshire Republican who escaped communist China, warns a Democratic Congress could let Beijing expand its influence in Washington.
articles.body: A congressional nominee who escaped communist China after the Tiananmen Square massacre warned that a Democratic-controlled Congress could create opportunities for Beijing to expand its influence in Washington, threatening U.S. national security. Lily Tang Williams, the Republican nominee for New Hampshire's 2nd Congressional District, told Fox News Digital that China, a country she believes "wants to bring down the United States," would capitalize on "America’s weakness" if Congress were to be controlled by Democrats in January. "I fear that the country I love is becoming the country I left," Williams, who is challenging Rep. Maggie Goodlander, D-N.H., told Fox News Digital. "China will be very happy to see Democrats control the House and Senate. The Democrats want open borders, they want to defund police and abolish private property. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) is looking at this as good news." CHINA EXPERT WARNS BEIJING WANTS AMERICANS — NOT THE CCP — TO SPREAD ITS MESSAGE Williams pointed to a recent Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) trip, claiming that more than a dozen high-ranking members of the organization traveled to China to "produce favorable coverage of China and its regime," as an example of the Chinese government taking advantage of the "vulnerable Democratic Party" to promote itself in the U.S. "They now share a similar ideology," Williams said. DEMOCRATIC SOCIALISTS OF AMERICA NEED TO ACTUALLY MEET THE CHINA THEY CLAIM TO LOVE Williams also argued that Democrats' immigration policies could make it easier for Chinese intelligence operatives to enter the U.S., warning about the potential for espionage along the southern border. The candidate said she believes the DSA's growing influence within the Democratic Party could shape congressional decisions even if Democrats remain in the minority or more moderate lawmakers hold leadership positions. "The Democrat Party is hijacked by the DSA," Williams said. "We’re going to have a DSA-run Congress, whether moderate Democrats like it or not. Moderate Democrat voters are still so complacent. They don't come out and condemn this extremism because they may even be afraid of repercussions from the DSA and DSA voters." A recent Gallup poll found that 43% of Americans have a positive view of socialism, for the first time since 2010. Williams pointed to the rise of socialism among Americans and the possibility that at least six new DSA-affiliated lawmakers could enter Congress in January as reasons for concern about the direction of the Democratic Party. "Congress will be controlled by people who sympathize with the CCP and its Marxist principles," Williams warned. TOP DEM TORCHES SOCIALISTS TAKING OVER HIS PARTY: 'THEY'RE ANTI-AMERICAN' Williams also criticized her Democratic opponent and other members of the party for what she described as their refusal to condemn Marxism, arguing that moderate Democrats could increasingly side with the party's progressive wing in the 120th Congress. "Our country could fall from within, because we don't really have a good policy to protect ourselves and our national security," Williams said. "My opponent refuses to condemn Marxism and Marxist American figures like New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani when asked. This is very troubling." During her phone interview with Fox News Digital, Williams raised concerns that lawmakers sympathetic to Marxist ideology could pose national security risks if they gained access to sensitive or classified information. articles.title: Former Obama aide declares Jewish Michiganders have a 'moral obligation' to support El-Sayed
articles.summary: Jon Lovett says Jewish voters in Michigan have a "moral obligation" to back Abdul El-Sayed, sparking fierce pushback from critics.
articles.body: Former Obama aide Jon Lovett urged Jewish Michiganders to vote for Abdul El-Sayed, saying voters have a "moral obligation" to support the Democratic U.S. Senate nominee in Michigan. On Tuesday's episode of the "Pod Save America" podcast, the co-host condemned President Donald Trump for his rhetoric about El-Sayed at a recent rally for GOP candidate Mike Rogers. Lovett urged Jewish voters in Michigan to reject Trump's rhetoric, arguing that antisemitism on the left paled in comparison to the "hatred" coming from the right, which he said would eventually make America less safe for Jewish people. "So Donald Trump says there that any Jew would be ashamed to vote for Abdul, and there's a debate among Jews in Michigan about whether to vote for Abdul. I just want to be very clear, Jews in Michigan have a moral obligation to support Abdul," he said. "They should do it to protect themselves from antisemitism and rising hatred in America." 'POD SAVE AMERICA' HOSTS WARN EL-SAYED TO TONE DOWN 'CONDESCENSION' ON MUSLIM BROTHERHOOD QUESTIONS "And if that sounds confusing to you at all, you should imagine two futures," he continued. "One in which there is a debate inside the Democratic Party about America's relationship to Israel, military aid for Israel and antisemitism on the left, which is real. That is a big and important debate we could have to try to find places of agreement, places of consensus. There can be persuasion and argument and hard feelings, but there can be democracy." The other future, Lovett said, would be dangerous for Jewish people. "On the other, you have this kind of politics on the right, where it is about dominance and hatreds and othering of people. It starts with Muslims," he said. "He does it for trans people. He does it for immigrants. He does it for Haitians, eating the dogs and the cats. If you think that that doesn't end with Jews, you are out of your f---ing minds." "A country where this kind of politics is rewarded is a country where Jews are less safe. And anyone who has allowed their own concerns and legitimate concerns about Abdul to cloud that ultimate larger point is missing the big picture here," Lovett continued. "For Jews in America, our safety is based around the idea that there's a society in which we can have arguments and disagreements, but we respect those differences. Trump does not believe in that. And we need to have a check on Donald Trump in a Democratic Senate. And maybe Abdul is not your cup of tea. Maybe Abdul is not — is going to be a reliable vote against Israel. Fine, we can handle that. But we cannot handle a continued slide to this hateful authoritarian right. It will be dangerous for us." JEWISH DEMOCRATS ABANDON EL-SAYED FOR GOP RIVAL IN ALL-IMPORTANT BATTLEGROUND STATE Manhattan Institute Vice President Jesse Arm, a pollster and Michigan native, wrote to Fox News Digital about Lovett's comments. "Jon Lovett is a bitterly partisan hack who backed a candidate in Maine with a literal Nazi symbol inked on his chest because he had a D next to his name. He’s in no position to lecture Jews about their moral obligations," he said, appearing to refer to former Maine Democratic Senate candidate Graham Platner, who suspended his campaign in July following a sexual assault allegation, which he denied. articles.title: Trump revisits 10-year warning to Macron as protests sweep France: ‘You have to get them out’
articles.summary: Donald Trump told Emmanuel Macron for a decade that France would "lose" its country without addressing the immigration crisis fueling protests.
articles.body: President Donald Trump revisited his longstanding warning to French President Emmanuel Macron that France could "lose" its country if it doesn’t address immigration troubles. "It's not a school problem. It's an immigration problem," Trump told Fox News Digital Tuesday night after rallying in Texas in a final push for Republicans ahead of next week's midterms. "I've been saying that to President Macron for a long time, who I like a lot, by the way. But I said, ‘You're going to end up losing your country if you don't do something.’" Trump’s call for France to close its borders follows student demonstrations that have devolved into widespread protests over local grievances, packing streets, sparking clashes and ricocheting across Europe. TRUMP REVEALS DIRE WARNING TO MACRON AS VIOLENT UNREST SPREADS ACROSS EUROPE During a conversation with U.S. Ambassador to France Charles Kushner earlier this week, Trump told Fox News Digital they discussed France’s immigration problems, which he believes were behind the protests. "You have people that hate France," he said. "They hate the buildings, hate the art, they hate the people. And they're in there, and you have to get them out." Trump called the situation in France and across Europe "very sad," saying his warnings to Macron have spanned a decade. "Something has to happen, and they better do something," he said. "I’ve been saying it for 10 years, too." Trump has raised concerns about immigration in Europe for roughly a decade, dating back to his first presidential campaign in 2016. Macron became France's president in 2017. VIOLENT FAR-LEFT RIOTS IN FRANCE ARE 'CHILLING WARNING' FOR AMERICANS AT HOME, MIKE JOHNSON SAYS Trump has previously credited his own immigration policies with preventing similar unrest in the U.S. Macron accused foreign leaders last week of making "unacceptable and even stupid" comments, calling them false claims for political gain. He did not mention Trump or Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu by name — both the U.S. and Israel are in the midst of high-stakes election cycles. In France, French Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez said "nearly 1,000 people" were arrested Saturday as nationwide protests resumed. Macron said "ultra-left groups whose aim is to bring down the Republic" are leading the protests and that those organized by "individuals or groups with no legitimate authority" would be banned. FRANCE'S MACRON BLAMES PROTESTS ON 'ULTRA-LEFT GROUPS WHOSE AIM IS TO BRING DOWN THE REPUBLIC' Remaining on high alert, Macron said anyone who loots or damages property will be forced to pay, as tens of thousands of police were deployed. A Fox News Digital investigation identified 50 Antifa groups among nearly 300 groups mobilizing around the protests, as well as a sprawling network of communist, socialist, far-left and anti-Israel groups. Protests also spiraled in other parts of Europe this month, with violence breaking out in Rome and Albania’s capital, Tirana, where demonstrators set government buildings on fire. articles.title: Long-running embassy fight comes back to haunt Trump as State Dept hit with $461M lawsuit
articles.summary: B.L. Harbert International alleges the State Department reached a $370 million settlement over COVID-19 embassy construction claims, then reversed course.
articles.body: FIRST ON FOX — The latest lawsuit launched against the Trump administration seeks to recover more than $461 million after the State Department directed a longtime embassy builder to continue construction projects worldwide through the COVID-19 pandemic. B.L. Harbert International, which has built dozens of U.S. embassies and consulates over more than two decades, reached a $370 million settlement with the State Department to handle resulting claims — but the compnay claims the deal was reversed after current political leadership intervened. The builders are now seeking to recover lost funding through suing the Trump administration, and filed a lawsuit on Wednesday in the U.S. Court of Federal Claims, Fox News Digital first learned. The complaint covers 12 diplomatic construction projects across four continents, including facilities in Turkey, Iraq, Thailand, Morocco, Mexico and Central America. The company alleges career State Department officials reached the $370 million agreement in September 2025, but the government paid just $501,636 before backing out. Harbert claims political leadership "inserted themselves into the process after a settlement was reached" and that the decision to abandon it "came from the top." "We did not want to take this step. The U.S. Government is an important partner, and we are proud of the work we do together to advance America's interests and protect Americans serving overseas," Charles Bohn, president of BL Harbert's International Group, said in a statement. TRUMP ADMINISTRATION UNCOVERS $1.2B IN SUSPECTED COVID CONTRACT FRAUD TIED TO BIDEN-ERA SPENDING "But we have a responsibility to our employees and to the future of that mission. We kept our commitment under extraordinarily difficult conditions. We are asking the government to keep its commitment to us." Harbert is one of a small pool of U.S. contractors capable of building highly secure diplomatic facilities overseas — work that requires specialized security clearances, vetted workforces and the ability to manage complex construction and supply chains abroad. According to the company, some State Department embassy projects now draw just two or three qualified bidders. The dispute stretches across three presidential administrations, beginning with State Department directives issued during Trump's first term in 2020, continuing as Harbert pursued compensation during the Biden administration and culminating in the alleged settlement and its collapse during Trump's second term. At the beginning of the Covid-19 pandemic, Harbert was working on 17 embassy and consulate construction projects around the world, representing nearly two-thirds of State's embassy construction program at the time, according to the lawsuit. As countries shut down and global supply chains seized up in early 2020, Harbert says it sought guidance from State on whether to pause construction. The company argues the pandemic constituted an "excusable delay" under its contracts that would have allowed it to send personnel home, secure construction sites and resume work once conditions stabilized. Instead, Harbert alleges State decided to keep its overseas construction program moving. The company says State directed it to remain ready to mobilize, continue procuring and shipping materials and work through the disruptions, while instructing Harbert to document the resulting costs and submit requests for reimbursement. In one March 2020 communication cited in the complaint, Harbert warned State that it could not afford to continue paying workers to remain on standby without assurances of reimbursement. Labor costs on the new U.S. Embassy in Guatemala City alone were running roughly $1.3 million per month, according to the filing. Weeks later, State directed Harbert to "continue to procure and ship materials" so projects would not end up at the "back of the line" when global construction activity resumed, the complaint alleges. State recognized that doing so could generate additional storage, shipping and other costs and directed the company to submit requests for equitable adjustments as those costs arose, according to the filing. The projects ultimately moved forward under pandemic restrictions that Harbert says increased costs and reduced productivity as the company dealt with workforce limitations, supply-chain disruptions and new operating requirements. The government has since taken possession of all 12 diplomatic facilities at issue in the lawsuit and has been using some of them for more than three years, according to Harbert. Harbert ultimately submitted more than $500 million in requests for equitable adjustments and other claims stemming from the pandemic directives and separate project disputes, including alleged design changes and government-caused delays. OBAMA CENTER SUBCONTRACTOR SHUTS DOWN AMID $4M FIGHT, LAYS OFF 25 Harbert alleges members of State Department political leadership "inserted themselves into the process after a settlement was reached" and that, "on information and belief," the decision to abandon the agreement "came from the top." Fox News Digital has reached out to the State Department for comment. With deadlines approaching to preserve its claims, Harbert says it formally certified them in March 2026. The complaint alleges State's chief of staff encouraged the company to do so, representing that certification would make it easier for the government to implement the settlement. Instead, State contracting officers began denying the claims in July. By Oct. 13, 2026, all 13 certified claims now at issue in the lawsuit had received final decisions. Harbert is now seeking at least $461,097,380 in damages, along with interest and other relief. The lawsuit does not currently ask the court to enforce the alleged $370 million settlement itself. Harbert says its settlement-related claims remain in the administrative process and that it reserves the right to add them to the lawsuit later. The dispute could carry consequences beyond the hundreds of millions of dollars at stake. Harbert has been awarded roughly 60 U.S. embassy and consulate construction projects since 1999. The company says the number of American contractors willing and qualified to undertake such work has dwindled significantly, in some cases leaving just two or three qualified bidders for projects. Embassy construction requires contractors to meet stringent security and workforce-vetting requirements while managing highly specialized construction, secure facilities and international logistics, creating significant barriers for companies seeking to enter the field.
